en: Preface to the *Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra:

Rectifying Errors* The Prajñāpāramitā is the ultimate emptiness; the Vajra is its wondrous meaning. It enables people to awaken to their own original nature and realize their own fundamental mind, thereby suddenly shedding the myriad disturbances of the sense organs and their objects.
Only when one can empty all bodily forms may one begin to provide an exegesis; for all such commentaries flow from one’s own mind.
It emerges, perfectly bright, pure, and wondrous, exactly like the brilliant sun, illuminating many thousands of Buddha-lands without leaving even a single valley in shadow.

Now, regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, there are differences among five translations; however, that first translated by Kumārajīva of the Qin dynasty alone has been widely circulated and remains prevalent in the world.
My fellow townsman, Mr. Zhong Zishí, studied the various classics and ancient texts of the sages of the Zhòu and Lǔ traditions from his youth, and in his later years...
He inquired into the profound essentials of the various scriptures of India and frequently recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, forgetting the passage of years and months.
Wisdom arose within him, and he scrutinized dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows as being false and delusive; he no longer regarded the concepts of self, person, multitude, or life-span as real.
Having realized that their fundamental source is signless (*animitta*), he compiled various commentaries, excising the redundant and simplifying the essential.

He elucidated the meanings and corrected errors, like hanging a golden mirror upon a high terrace where both beauty and ugliness are fully revealed; or like gathering all rivers into the vast ocean, overflowing with clarity and purity.
Regardless of whether one is a monastic or a layperson, upon reading this, all will clearly understand supreme bodhi.

Having obtained the opportunity during the reign of King [Ji], I, Guangwen, who have long been devoted to the study of Chan, have collated and scrutinized the text. I have gathered together various faithful donors to carve it for printing so that it may circulate widely.

Should it meet with another Great Mirror (Huineng) who, upon hearing the recitation of "because there is no place to dwell," suddenly awakens to their original nature, then the merit of this endeavor will not be slight.
You should understand that which lies beyond words; know that returning to the natural state means that even empty space vanishes away.
If you seek the marks of letters, they are utterly unobtainable. This is truly entering the inconceivable. May readers believe and accept these words, for only then will there be attainment.
Preface to the *Jingang jing zhuzheng'e* (Correcting Errors in the Commentary on the Diamond Sutra).
It has been over seventeen hundred years since the Sanskrit texts of Western India arrived in our land of China. Those who have grasped their essential meaning have clarified them.

The original nature has been restored; there have been enlightened and wise minds throughout the ages. The text appears free from errors or corruptions. For instance, regarding the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*:
since Kumārajīva translated it in Chang’an, it was titled "Śrāvastī. Subsequently, a branch translation was first produced in Luoyang, titled "Śāvatthī.
Paramārtha translated it again at the Jetavana Grove, and Buddhabhadra translated it a third time at...

Regarding the "Jetavana" (祇陀林), Xuanzang later translated it as "Śrāvastī Forest" (誓多林). Now, among these five translations, are the wording and meaning truly so perfectly concordant that they are like two halves of a tally?
If they are indeed identical, what need is there for multiple translations?
If they are not, then as for those who claim "this one is correct and that one is wrong," which way shall we turn? This truly opens a fissure for error. Furthermore—
Since the commentaries of Xie Lingyun and Tan Chen on the *Shi yi* (Explanation of Terms), more than a hundred schools have emerged over the past decades.

Yet, those currently circulating in the world are merely the works of the three masters Zhongfeng, Guifeng, and Changshui. However, are the commentaries of the two "Peaks" truly superior to those of Master Xie?

And is the discourse of Changshui more excellent than that of the two Peaks? Is it not so? In my view, regarding the commentaries on the Five Classics, the traditions of Zhu Xi and Cheng Yi are held in the highest esteem.
This requires Zhu Xi and Cheng Hao; it is likewise a matter of "divining what is covered.

If a person of a hundred generations hence could be of one accord with the mind of those of a hundred generations past, matching them perfectly as one, then why would "seeing and knowing" be so prized?

Moreover, regarding the "insect-script" and "bird-seal" characters from ten thousand *li* away and a thousand years prior, if one wishes to interpret their mental methods (*xinfa*), even if that person were to be reborn and examine themselves, they would not [be able to do so].
Do not hold that the present is right while the past was wrong, yet desire to cling to your own views in order to claim the seal of approval for the intentions of those who came before you.
This is like chasing a shadow; the more you exert yourself, the faster the shadow flees. It is no wonder, then, that errors increase day by day.

I humbly wish that those who read the Golden Sutra would neither flatter Buddhism while slandering Confucianism, nor revere Confucianism while excluding Buddhism; do not use Confucianism to propagate Buddhism, nor use Buddhism [to propagate Confucianism].
The "mud Confucian" should interpret Confucianism through Confucianism; this is precisely like using Buddhism to verify Buddhism.

To summarize the essential purport of the entire *Golden Sūtra*, it should be nothing other than the single phrase, "abide thus. How could this differ in degree from the words in the *Book of Yu*: "settle your stillness"?
It is truly a matter of people forcibly creating distinctions—this is like a clay figurine laughing at a wooden puppet. Shu Ruozhong was a renowned Confucian scholar;
regarding the Classics and the Histories, there was nothing he did not pluck for its fragrance or gather for its blossoms.
Beyond the hours spent by lamp and dew in study, he extensively hunted through the Golden Sūtras, correcting every error of punctuation, every error of phonology, and every error of interpretation.

May those who recite and study it find its brilliance like a torch of fire. Its merit should be equal to that of Ding Hong’s collation of the differences among the Five Classics at the White Tiger Hall;
it may truly be called a "Lion of the Sutras and Tiger of the Vinaya. Nevertheless, I privately harbor a doubt:

when the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, he took the non-reliance on words and letters as his primary principle at the Deer Park—a tradition my own school has long upheld. Now, how can you, my worthy son, [proceed] with this?

I write this to verify our agreement regarding the practice of *dhyāna*. I fear that you may remain to my left [in spiritual rank]. Some say that those whose karmic merit lies in wisdom and literature should be reborn in the heavens;
you, my second son, possess both a mind of wisdom and a tongue of wisdom—this is indeed the karma of wisdom.
As for me, who does not rely on written words, I stand even further behind you, my second son. How can I bear it? I beg you for a single word to correct my errors; would you grant this?

In the sixth month of the Bingchen year of the Kangxi era, his fellow student Xu Laibin Jiuyifu respectfully inscribed this title for the *Jingang jing zhu zheng'e* (Corrections of Errors in the Commentary on the Diamond Sutra).
Compiled by Qing Changshui Zhongzhiping Shishifufu.
Tiandu Wang Weixin, on this occasion, has corrected the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
This sutra was spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha; it was compiled by Ānanda and Kāśyapa and transmitted to the world. Gold... [End of fragment]
It is the treasure of all things. Its nature is most firm; it does not change when encountering fire. This is a metaphor for the true nature of humans, which remains indestructible throughout kalpas.
*Prajñā* means wisdom; *pāra* means the other shore. A mind of clear and penetrating wisdom can sever all attachments;
this is precisely the indestructible body of the Vajra. It is not merely physical strength like that of gold.

"Vajra" means that such wisdom does not exist [in ordinary beings]; hence it is called the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*. When the mind is deluded, one is on this shore; when the mind is awakened, one is on the other shore.
Sentient beings drift through birth and death, never leaving this shore. If they can diligently cultivate *prajñā*, [they shall reach the other shore].
Leaving this shore of birth and death, one immediately reaches the other shore of nirvāṇa. Non-abiding prajñā is itself the other shore of nirvāṇa;
there is no other shore apart from prajñā. "Mi" (蜜) is taught as harmony, for it unifies the single nature with all natures.
"Jing" (經) is taught as the path; the Buddha uses verbal teachings to clarify the path of the mind, which transcends birth.

This is the shortcut to death. For one who possesses the roots of goodness, beginning with the recitation of the sutra and ending with the realization of its principle, they attain the power of firmness;
this is the Vajra. Possessing great wisdom, this is Prajñā. Crossing the ocean of birth and death and ascending to the shore of Bodhi, this is the Pāramitā.
Since the entire sutra expounds the wondrous meaning of Prajñā, the Tathāgata has designated it as such.
The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Chapter One: The Origin of the Dharma Assembly.
This sūtra consists of thirty-two divisions, which were established by Xiao Tong, the Prince of昭明 (Zhāomíng), during the Liang dynasty. From here on...
This refers to the preparation of the seats; it is the place where the assembly for the preaching of the Dharma gathers, and is thus called the "causal basis of the Dharma assembly.

"Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), from this point up to "five hundred people together," constitutes the general introduction to this sutra. "Thus" (*evam*) has the meaning of "approximating" or "reproducing. This...
"Those" is a term used for identification, referring to what is stated in a particular scripture.

Regarding the statement that "in the Buddha-dharma there is no self," the term "self" is used here with reference to the person who expounds the Buddha-dharma; it is Ānanda and Kāśyapa speaking of themselves.

"Hearing" refers to the arising of consciousness through the faculty of the ear, whereby wisdom and understanding are produced in dependence upon those names and phrases. This is because when Ānanda ascended the seat to preach the Dharma...
This means that regarding what is stated in this sutra— namely, "I have heard such a Dharma from the Buddha at a certain place among a certain assembly"—
this was not originally a product of one's own speculative discourse.
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Because the calendars of the Western Heavens and the Eastern Lands differ regarding the beginning of the year, the specific month and day are not indicated; it simply says "at one time.
This refers to the occasion when the conditions for teaching this Prajñāpāramitā converged. Since the temporal cycles of various regions differ in their duration and brevity, [the date] is merely...
Regarding the term "One": "Buddha" means awakening. Internally, he is awakened to the absence of all deluded thoughts; externally, he is awakened to being unstained by the six sense objects.
Having awakened himself and awakened others, and having perfected the practice of awakening, he alone is called Buddha—namely, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha.
His name was Siddhārtha; his father was King Śuddhodana, and his mother was Māyā. The phrase "is located" clarifies its position:
it was there that he happened to plant his staff, rather than making it his permanent residence. The kingdom of Śrāvastī lies to the east of India in the Western Regions;
it was the seat of King Prasenajit. The Jeta Grove was planted by Jeta, the prince of that king, and was thus named after him.
"Named Anāthapiṇḍada. This is the courtesy name of the elder Sudatta, a minister of King Bimbisāra. The garden was originally the park of Prince Jeta;
because Sudatta constantly gave alms to the solitary and the poor within it, it was consequently named Anāthapiṇḍada (Giver of Alms to the Destitute).
Sudatta invited the Buddha to preach the Dharma, and the Buddha instructed him to first select an excellent site. Only Prince Jeta...
The Prince’s Garden was square, vast, and immaculate. [Sudatta] went to inform the Prince, who said in jest, "If you spread gold to fill the garden, I shall sell it to you.
Sudatta returned home and transported gold, spreading it side-by-side over eighty *qǐng*; the garden was completely covered.
The Prince would no longer accept the gold, and they together constructed the Jetavana Vihāra, inviting the Buddha to reside there and preach the Dharma. (Two verses)
The narrator, based on what he had heard and seen, attests that the Tathāgata appeared in person to preach the Dharma,
together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
"Together with" (*sārdham*) has the sense of including others. "Bhikṣu" is a term for a disciple. One who abandons evil and adopts good is a junior bhikṣu;
one who has cast off both good and evil is called a senior bhikṣu. They are called "senior" because they have thoroughly mastered the principles, like disciples of a high seat;
these are of the class of Arhats. "Assembly" (*saṃgha*) refers to the harmony of both principle and phenomena; though numerous, they are as one.
Furthermore, when the Buddha attained enlightenment, he first ordained the five men, including Kauṇḍinya; next, he ordained the three Kāśyapas along with their thousand followers;
next, he ordained Śāriputra and his hundred followers; next, he ordained Maudgalyāyana and his hundred followers;
and then the householder Yaśas and his fifty followers. At each of these dharma assemblies, they constantly followed the Buddha without ever leaving him. Therefore...
At the beginning of various sūtras, the great assembly is enumerated, all stating that they were "together with one thousand two hundred and fifty people.

"Together" (jù) means being in the same location within the grove to listen to the Dharma. This indicates that the Buddha was at this site and that those who followed him were numerous; it refers to seeing the place where the various transformed disciples reside.
At that time, at the hour of eating, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food;
this serves as the introductory narrative. At that very moment, because the Buddha is the Honored One of the world, he is called the World-Honored One (Bhagavān).
The various devas eat in the morning, the various spirits eat in the evening, and the Buddhas eat at midday. "The hour of eating" refers to noon.
At the juncture of the previous hour of Si (around noon), those who wore robes donned the *kāṣāya*, the garment of patience;
those who carried bowls took up the bowl transmitted by Vipaśyin Buddha. Thus, manifesting the traces of his teaching, he set forth.
As for "entering," he entered from outside the city into the great city of Śrāvastī, the city of abundant virtue within the kingdom of Śrāvastī, namely that of King Prasenajit.

Although he resided as a prince, he humbled himself by begging for alms; this was intended to break his own arrogance, to transform and inspire sentient beings, and to ensure that bhikṣus of future generations would not accumulate wealth and treasures.

Having completed his almsround through the city in due order, he returned to his dwelling. When he had finished his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, prepared his seat, and sat down.
Regarding "begging in sequence": it is not that the Tathāgata goes alone to beg; he is accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty followers.
When Kāśyapa went on his alms-round, he bypassed the wealthy to follow the poor, seeking to create merit for the destitute.
When Subhūti went on his alms-round, he bypassed the poor to approach the wealthy, seeking to make giving easier for the affluent. The Buddha rebuked both of them. "In sequence" means equality.
In treating others, there is no selection or discrimination; one does not bypass the poor to follow the wealthy, nor abandon the lowly to follow the noble.

One proceeds in sequence until everyone is reached. Having provided for oneself with enough food for a single day, one begins the following day with those who have not yet begged, and only then does one proceed to reach everyone.
Seeing the Buddha as he was, there was no sense of haste or urgency. "Already" means completion; once the begging is finished, it is done.
Without retaining even a trace of the thought that [the practice] was not yet complete, he returns to his original location—namely, Jeta’s Grove—and proceeds to the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden to eat.
By this time, all those who had been waiting to hear the Dharma have finished their meals. The character "to collect" (shōu) corresponds to the two characters "to wear" and "to hold" mentioned above;
it refers to putting away the *kāṣāya* robe and washing the alms bowl. On this day, one does not go out again.

Regarding "washing the feet": the Buddha walked barefoot; he would wash them with water to purify his physical karma and mind, washing away the defilements of afflictions (*kleśa*) and manifesting the pure *dharmakāya*.
Therefore, the Saṃgha refers to him as "White-footed" (*Śvetapāda*). Regarding "spreading": it means to lay out.

One spreads the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) and sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) to rest properly and enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*). For if one lies down, there is dullness (*styāna*), and if one walks, there is agitation (*auddhatya*).

[The Master] raised his hand: "When sitting, one becomes weary; only the full-lotus posture (paryaṅka) constitutes the True Dharma. The physical form of the Buddha is upright and majestic; he does not look left or right in this manner.
This passage describes the World-Honored One at the proper time and measure, clearly manifesting the profound Prajñā-pāramitā, which is not apart from ordinary daily life.
The Buddha directly [attained it] from within the act of begging for alms and sitting in meditation. And so forth...
He laid it out upon his palm to reveal the fundamental nature, so that one might witness the Way as it exists.

On the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, the year of Jiayin, the well-springs overflowed, the palaces shook, and at night the fixed stars were no longer visible.
The Grand Historian Su Yao divined that a sage from the West had been born; was this not the birth and descent of Śākyamuni?
○ Section Two: The Request of Subhūti.
Subhūti first praised the Tathāgata and subsequently posed his questions; hence it is called "The Request of Subhūti."
"At that time, the Elder Subhūti.
Regarding "at that time," it refers to the moment when Subhūti arose to pose his question. One who is venerable in virtue and advanced in years is called an "Elder" (*sthavira*).

He is seen as distinct from the other bhikṣus. "Subhūti" is a term in the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "Born of Emptiness" (*Kūṭastha*). He is also named "Well-Appeared" (*Suvibhakta*), because—

He suddenly realized the nature of quiescent emptiness; this is truly Bodhi, and thus he is named Subhūti. Because he can give rise to the myriad things within emptiness, he is named Kōshō (Empty-Born).
Because the nature of emptiness manifests in accordance with conditions to benefit people and things, he is also named Zen-gen (Good Manifestation).
All those who engaged in dialogue with Śākyamuni were such as these; it was not limited to a single person.
In the midst of the great assembly, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The practitioner seeks nothing else; therefore it is said, 'in the midst of the great assembly,' namely the twelve hundred and fifty [bhikṣus]."

This is within the human realm. The great assembly sat down because they were listening to the Dharma; Subhūti alone rose from among the seated monks and requested the teaching, from this point until the section on "reverence.
This constitutes a disciple requesting the Dharma, wherein he first performs the five kinds of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).
This refers to the sincerity of the three karmas. In the northern lands, one bares the shoulder when repenting and asking for forgiveness;
in the western lands, one bares the shoulder when showing reverence and performing rites. At that time, the garment worn is draped over the right shoulder while the left is bared.
Such is the standard style of clothing throughout the Western Regions; it is not Subhūti alone who wears it in this manner. Placing the right knee on the ground is what is meant by "kneeling" today.
Regarding the ritual (li): the omission of the word "left" is for the sake of brevity. The right is the path of correctness; the left is the path of deviation.

Since the correct can eliminate the deviant, the customs of the Western Land (India) esteem the right as a mark of reverence. Joining the palms in reverence is simply a means of seeking the World-Honored One’s intention to preach the Dharma.
"To announce" (bai) refers to the formal declaration (biao-bai).
"How rare, World-Honored One!
Subhūti does not inquire impulsively; he first uses words of praise for the Buddha to move him with sincerity, and only then does he pose his request.
'How rare' means that the Buddha-nature encompasses all phenomena, which is beyond the reach of ordinary people, O World-Honored One."
This person’s wisdom transcends the triple world; his sanctity is such that none can equal it; his virtue is unsurpassed and supreme, and all pay him reverence.
From within the most ordinary of daily activities, he perceives through and through those who are most extraordinary throughout the ages.
The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all bodhisattvas and skillfully entrusts all bodhisattvas.
Since he is called "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) and also called "Tathāgata," the latter is indeed a title for a Buddha that may be used as a general designation.
"Coming" (*lai*) is the essential function of true nature; it responds and communicates with all beings, manifesting without exception.
Speaking in terms of both the essence and function of the Buddha, the two phrases concerning "protective mindfulness" (*hu nian*) refer precisely to what is called a rare and marvelous event.
This first describes the Buddha’s habitual practice to evoke his compassion. As for "protecting" (*hu*):
"Affectionately protecting" (*anurakṣaṇā*) means to keep in mind. This refers to how the Tathāgata’s compassion is profound and heavy;

toward those who have heard the Dharma from him—whether kin or not—he applies himself with special care and concern, bestowing the power of wisdom so that they may achieve self-perfection, and bestowing the power of transformation so that they may likewise deliver sentient beings.
"Entrusting" (*parindana*) means to commit; "instructing" (*anuśāsana*) means to exhort earnestly. This refers to how the Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom is clear and pure.

For those in the world and future generations who were unable to hear [the teachings] directly from him, he was able to instruct and reveal them with thorough detail and repeated precision, causing them all to attain realization.
He entrusted the great to the small, bestowing upon them predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*); he charged the great to protect the small, ensuring their success.

As for the two instances of praising them as "excellent," one must understand that this was according to their capacities; since he did not lead them through forced effort, how could it be merely a matter of sound?
He sought [it] through form, yet he merely provided a final model by means of gradual and skillful guidance. "All" (zhū) signifies non-unity.
"Buo" (菩) means illumination; "sa" (薩) means seeing. This Bodhisattva is a Bodhisattva who has first resolved his mind [upon enlightenment].
These are precisely the good sons and good daughters mentioned above. In its original Sanskrit, it is *bodhisattva*;

here, the text has been abbreviated to "Bosatsu" (Bodhisattva) for the sake of ease in address. *Bodhi* translates into Chinese as "awakening" (*jue*), and *sattva* translates as "sentient being" (*youqing*).
Thus, "Awakened Sentient Being" refers to one who is capable of giving rise to virtuous thoughts, yet whose [deluded] existence is not yet severed.
It refers to sentient beings (*sattva*). If one reaches the stage of Buddhahood, one is simply called "Awakened" (*buddha*), and the term "sentient being" is no longer used.
As for the various Bodhisattvas, they are those among humanity who possess sentience and are oriented toward goodness; therefore, the Buddha protected them and entrusted them with his teachings.

"World-Honored One! Whenever good sons or good daughters have a question to pose, they first address the World-Honored One to express their reverence. These following four phrases mark the beginning of the inquiry.
Regarding 'good sons and daughters,' those who are outside the assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty people are intended; as for 'sons,' this includes [all males]."

The three assemblies of śrāmaṇeras, upāsakas, and bhikṣus; and the four assemblies of women—bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsikās, and śikṣamāṇās—are those referred to at the end of the sutra as "bhikṣus, upāsakas," and so forth.
The Buddha desired to extensively deliver both men and women, leading them all toward the good.
"Having resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind?
The character "should" (*ying*) appears above "how" (*yunhe*) in the editions of Li Tengfang, Zhu Chongqu, and others; this is furthermore profound.
I maintain this heart of entrustment in order to seek your instruction. If ordinary people possess this heart yet sink into emotional desires, they will be unable to bring it forth.
It is like a sprout just beginning to bud that is obscured by other things; though it wishes to grow, it cannot do so.
"To bring forth" refers to the sprouting of the seed, following its natural emergence. The character "Ā" (阿) is used as an auxiliary particle.
Regarding the terminology: *anuttara* means "unsurpassed" (*wu shang*). *Samyak* means "perfectly equal" (*zheng deng*). *Saṃbodhi* means "perfect awakening" (*zheng jue*).
This refers to the true nature (*tathatā*) which rises above all worldly desires—this is "unsurpassed. It is fully present in every single thing—this is "perfectly equal.

Its radiance shines everywhere, unobscured by the defilements of karmic conditions—this is "perfect awakening. The character *shang* (upper) in *shang zheng* (upper-perfect) is to be understood as the character *zheng* (to realize/attest). Below...

The character "zheng" (正) is interpreted as "zhong" (中), meaning "the center. This refers to how men and women, having given rise to this wholesome thought, manage the myriad changes encountered in their daily lives with such ease, composure, and tranquility that they draw near to spontaneity (*ziran*).

Within the state of non-abiding, it is as if there is something to abide in. "Abiding" (*zhu*) carries the meaning of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Where there is true mind, there is likewise deluded mind.

Whenever a state of deviant mind arises in succession, one must subdue it through the power of great awakening—just as one restrains a venomous dragon, binds a fierce tiger, or wards off a powerful bandit.
If one is even slightly unable to subdue it, one will instead be struck by it; for that which dwells within is eternal.
Thus, that which is suppressed will be subtly eliminated and silently transformed. These two lines seek a path for entering the gate.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! As you have said, the Tathāgata skillfully protects and mindfully sustains all bodhisattvas."
[Sā]riputra. [The Buddha] has well entrusted the bodhisattvas.
What Subhūti has asked is urgent for the cultivation of the mind and perfectly accords with the Buddha’s intention; therefore, the Buddha approves it, saying:
"You have well grasped my heart! You have well grasped my meaning! Thus, having praised him as being correct, he further addresses him and reiterates his teaching.
"Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you.
To listen attentively means to thoroughly comprehend the sense-object of sound, not to pursue the words, but to listen with careful discernment. The Buddha was about to speak.
The Dharma. He always first exhorted and commanded that those listening should maintain single-minded silence, saying:
"I shall explain the subtle and profound essence to you in full detail; what I speak shall all be the ultimate truth. This refers to what is stated in the following passage.
Sons and daughters of good family who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide in this manner and thus subdue their minds.

The Buddha answered according to what was asked, saying: "All male and female bodhisattvas who wish to practice and give rise to the unsurpassed, true, and correct mind that knows no dharma unknown—of this I have a principle to teach you.
You should abide in this state of the Prajñā-dharma, which is neither excessive nor deficient, exactly reaching this stage. As it is said:
This is the Dharma of Prajñā. All demonic obstacles and evil paths are completely incinerated and returned to their place of abiding, thereby subduing the mind of deluded thought.
These two phrases must be read together as they point forward to the meaning of the answer provided in the subsequent text.
It is not merely dwelling in one-pointedness of mind; it is also the subduing of the mind through one-pointedness.
For if one dwells in that which is appropriate to dwell upon, then that which is inappropriate to dwell upon will naturally be subdued.

This is something that cannot be accomplished by one who does not possess morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Morality prevents wrongdoing and stops evil; concentration is tranquility and immovability; wisdom is clear illumination and prior knowledge.
It is like the manifestation of myriad phenomena within the ocean; this requires the water to be clear. To achieve clarity, nothing surpasses stillness;

to achieve stillness, do not allow waves to arise. The ceasing of waves resembles ethical discipline (*śīla*); the stillness of the water resembles meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and the clarity of the water resembles wisdom (*prajñā*). As for the objects and forms that manifest, they are like reflections.
"Like wisdom that penetrates all phenomena, it is attained entirely through the state of abiding and the state of subduing.
So it is, World-Honored One; we wish to hear it.
As soon as the Buddha had spoken these words as a prologue, before he had yet elucidated the actual reality, Subhūti immediately understood.

Fearing that people in the future age might fail to perceive the physical marks of the Buddha and instead develop a mind of indolence upon merely hearing his words, he asked this question.

The Buddha told Subhūti: "Do not speak thus. In the five hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, who are able to give rise to faith in these chapters and verses, and who take them as the truth.
You should know that such persons have planted roots of goodness not under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas, but have already done so under immeasurable thousands of millions of Buddhas."

Regarding those who have planted various roots of goodness and, upon hearing these phrases, give rise to even a single thought of pure faith—the Buddha rebuked Subhūti, saying: "Do not speak of giving rise to 'true' faith.
Within these phrases, regardless of whether the era is distant or near, there shall be none who do not believe. The 'five hundred years' is merely a rough approximation used by the Tathāgata."
The cycles of the world undergo order and chaos once every five hundred years. It is at such times that [the Buddhas] appear to perform acts of transformation and deliverance;

this is why they regard five hundred years as the appointed period. Not only do I, in the present time, hear this Dharma-gate of Prajñāpāramitā and not consider it difficult, but even if the Tathāgata were to speak these words five hundred years prior [to the end of the cycle], [I would likewise find no difficulty].
After five hundred years, only the words will remain. Those who uphold the Buddha’s precepts and cultivate merit, upon encountering these passages, will be able to give rise to faith.
As for what you call "true faith," could there be anything else? It is precisely this that constitutes true faith.
When one Buddha appears in the world, he is called "One Buddha"; one should know that the roots of goodness of such a person are likewise singular.

It is already profound; it does not merely concern one or two virtuous persons, nor three, four, or five virtuous persons who maintain the precepts, cultivate merit, and attain these roots of goodness.
It concerns immeasurable numbers of virtuous persons, up to tens of millions of such beings.
One reaches the source and obtains this seed, which is deep-rooted and firmly established;
therefore, upon hearing these words and phrases, even within a single thought-moment of non-abiding, one gives rise to pure faith, believing that this sutra can eliminate all afflictions.
To achieve supramundane merit is the word of the Tathāgata; even though the world has long since passed and people have perished, it is still believed and followed—how much more so in recent times!
"True faith" (*śraddhā*) means being authentic and not false. "Pure faith" means being singular and unmixed.
When one reaches the state of ultimate pure faith, then even "true" is insufficient as a description. Regarding "faith" (*śraddhā*), there are four instances in the sutras.
This is the locus. First, such people who plant roots of goodness are difficult to find. Second, those who are able to remain detached from signs are rare.
Third, this praises the greatness of that person’s merit. Fourth, it serves to exhort and encourage sentient beings.

What was previously called "entrusting with careful protection" refers precisely to such people—namely, good sons and daughters, and all bodhisattvas—and causes them to enter into the [unconditioned].
This is the nirvana with remainder; their spiritual capacities are distinguished herein.
Subhūti, the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees all these sentient beings who shall obtain such immeasurable merit.
Why is this? These sentient beings no longer possess the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span;
they possess neither the mark of dharmas nor the mark of non-dharmas.
This very moment of pure faith is precisely the mind of equality between the Buddha and sentient beings.
From this day forward, the Tathāgata perceives future sentient beings who, through cultivation over successive kalpas, shall attain such immeasurable merit.
Why is this so? This phrase "immeasurable merit" is intended to clarify that point. Among the sentient beings of future generations, [he singles out...]
Those individuals who emerge from this are sentient beings of pure mind. Having been refined through past lives, they have exhausted all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) until nothing remains;

there is not even a hair’s breadth of delusive attachment. Not only are the marks of self and person (*ātma-pudgala-lakṣaṇa*) entirely empty, but the marks of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) and non-phenomena (*adharma-lakṣaṇa*) are likewise purified in their entirety.
Therefore, they attain the Tathāgata’s most profound knowledge and vision. Regarding "the absence of the mark of phenomena": it means that...
When expounding the Dharma according to the chapters and phrases, it is difficult not to become dogmatic; thus, there is the "unattached mind.

There is nothing that is not a dharma-characteristic, for dharmas are established to transmit the teachings and must not fail to be followed; thus, there is also the "non-unattached mind. All of these constitute pure faith.
Yet the nature of wisdom is itself the Tathāgata; this is why one obtains immeasurable merit.
Why is this? Because if these sentient beings allow their minds to grasp at signs, they will become attached to the notions of a self, a person, a being, and a life-span.

If one grasps at the marks of dharmas, one is attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. Why is this? If one grasps at the marks of non-dharmas, one is likewise attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Why must one be free from all marks? The following section expresses this through the method of contraposition.

If these sentient beings first possess a mark within their minds and grasp it—whether they take it as "self," or seek the Western Land, or seek rebirth in the heavens, or seek to become a human in a future life—they are then attached to the four marks and contemplate impurity. In this sentence, there is an extra character "wei" (to be).
This is because the four marks are fundamentally non-existent, yet I have personally created these marks for myself.

If one allows the mind to dwell upon worldly affairs, becoming biased toward existence and grasping at the characteristics of phenomena, one will perceive that the Dharma of Prajñāpāramitā exists externally to the mind;
thus, one becomes mired in dogmatism and finds it difficult to penetrate. Furthermore, by following worldly trends, one clings to the four marks and fails to maintain right mindfulness.

Regarding purity: if one is biased toward non-existence and recognizes it as a sign of non-dharma, grasping at it, thinking "I am not practicing the dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā*," then one clings to stubborn emptiness as a dharma and acts according to one's own whims. This is to be attached to the four marks and to contemplate impurity.
All such cases constitute failing to plant roots of goodness; how then could one attain pure faith and merit?
Therefore, one should not grasp at the Dharma, nor should one grasp at what is not the Dharma. For this reason, the Tathāgata has always said to you, bhikṣus:
"Understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like a raft. Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."
The preceding section has already used both direct and inverse statements to provide exhortation and warning; this section further concludes by declaring that grasping at [dharmas] is inappropriate.

Only the Dharma of the Tathāgata should not be viewed as either partial existence or partial non-existence. To depart from the Dharma is itself "non-Dharma. To grasp at the Dharma is to cling to existence;
to grasp at non-Dharma is to cling to non-existence. Therefore, one should not grasp at the Dharma, nor should one merely rely upon written texts.
[This is] a phrase. One should not grasp at what is not the Dharma, yet end up falling into annihilationism. This is precisely because of the meaning of this mark of non-abiding;
it is because one must not, by means of a mind of existence or non-existence, become attached [to anything].
Knowing this reason, this principle has not been spoken from this day forward alone. The Tathāgata has constantly said to his disciples: "You all listen now."
O Bhikṣus, you should know that the various dharmas of giving for the sake of delivering sentient beings, which I have taught, must not be relied upon;
they are like a boat or oar for crossing a river. The word "raft" (kulla) should be severed.
Once one has crossed over, the raft is abandoned. This is the case for those whose mind-essence is clear and pure, who contemplate emptiness and illuminate [reality].
Upon hearing these words, he attained sudden enlightenment. This is the metaphorical aspect. It is like a fish drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, the fish knows it for itself.

At this moment, no matter how one speaks of the profound or the subtle, even the most vast and divine supernatural powers are of no use whatsoever. Therefore, it is said: "Even dharmas should be relinquished.
This is precisely what is meant by "having caught the fish, one forgets the trap; having caught the hare, one forgets the snare. How much more so for that which is not [a dharma]?
The Dharma is fundamentally non-existent; how could one err by grasping it according to one's own subjective views?

It is precisely because one is able to relinquish it that one reaches the other shore and possesses such immeasurable merit. When explained in this way, the flow of the text is smooth and easy to understand.
If, however, one takes the phrase "like the parable of the raft" as the primary clause, the principle becomes difficult to reconcile. Below, [it says] "even the Dharma should be abandoned..."

Regarding the phrase "even dharma should be relinquished": how can one proceed with this? If one understands non-dharma as being demonic or heterodox, how could that be comparable to the realization of those who have already understood the relinquishing of the raft? The Tathāgata, in this context, speaks of the phrase "even dharma should be relinquished."
Furthermore, it transcends words and phrases. Having already deeply understood the preceding discourse on words and phrases, one gives rise to true faith.
