Unconditioned Dharmas. "The three realms are mind only" refers to their differentiation. "The myriad dharmas are consciousness only" refers to the mind being unconditioned.

Therefore, "nature" (svabhāva) is taught [to indicate] the essence of consciousness, and "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) are taught [to indicate] its distinctions. The general desire is for people to understand how characteristics return to nature and how evolving consciousness returns to the mind.
How, then, could there be any dharma or any teaching? For this reason, this section is titled "Neither Attainment nor Teaching."
“Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

Or has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti replied, “As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed dharma named *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata could [attain].”
[The Buddha] says:
This follows from the preceding statement that "even dharmas should be relinquished. This is a rhetorical objection raised to awaken Subhūti’s mind.

[The point is that] there is neither attainment nor teaching; this is a great pillar. It is because Subhūti doubted whether the Buddha attains bodhi and doubted whether the Buddha teaches the Dharma that [this objection is raised].
He then followed his lead and questioned him, saying: "What is in your mind now? Do you mean that the Way was attained under the tree, or that the Tathāgata did not attain Bodhi?
When he preached the Dharma to the assemblies, do you mean that the Tathāgata preached the Dharma or did not preach it?
Thus, the Dharma should not be abandoned. The word "ye" (耶) is an indeclinable particle used here as a term of inquiry; it is intended to test whether he understands or not.
Subhūti replied: "As I understand it, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) taught by the Buddha—the non-apprehension of all marks—if it were a fixed entity, it could be named and attained.
Yet this Dharma of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is supremely transformative and versatile;
it is without grasping and without attachment. How could there be a real characteristic that is called 'enlightenment' (*bodhi*)? Since there is none..."

That which can be attained can only be named; it can only be cultivated within one's nature and is difficult to explain with words. One responds according to the capacity of the interlocutor and answers as they strike upon the truth.
How could there be any real dharma for the Tathāgata to speak? This is simply to say that there is no Way to be realized and no dharma to be preached.
This is precisely what is meant by "understanding the meaning of what the Buddha has taught. Regarding the fact that dharmas cannot be fixed: it is not...

These are like a thousand threads and ten thousand strands—so numerous that they are difficult to settle. It is simply because everyone possesses this true awakening that one ought to proceed directly to the Unsurpassed.
Yet, if one becomes mired in dharmas, one immediately falls into a conceptual trap; thus, the nature of awakening is instead turned into a mire by those very dharmas.

The following phrase speaks of the single character "yi" (also). Seeing the Tathāgata as having attained it within oneself and comparing it to others, both emerge from the state of the true nature’s vital animation;
in neither case is there any established dharma that serves as a teaching. Regarding the four instances of "no attainment":
first, this is because there is originally no fixed dharma, and thus there is no attainment. Second, it is because the teacher [transmits] with the mind...
The transmission is not transmitted through words; therefore, there is nothing to be attained. Third, this Bodhi is one's own mind; how could it be attained from elsewhere?
Fourth, after the realization of the fruit, one returns to one's original reality; though it is attained, it is not called "attainment."
There are also four instances where there is no teaching: first, this is the Dharma which is not ultimately real, and thus even teaching is non-teaching;

second, the entry into principle through the profound and mysterious, wherein there is no room for speech; third, the entry into the gate where one has attained realization and no longer depends on teaching;
and fourth, awakening to ultimate emptiness, which is ineffable.
Why is this? All dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and ineffable; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
For what reason are there no fixed dharmas and no fixed teachings? It is because the Tathāgata reveals them to sentient beings, yet it is not that he does not teach the Dharma.
However, regarding the unsurpassed bodhi taught by the Tathāgata, there is no truly existent dharma; this cannot be [expressed] by a single...
The Dharma of concentration cannot be grasped, nor can it be explained by means of any fixed dharma. Since it is ungraspable, it is likewise inexpressible.
Reaching this point, one cannot say it is the Dharma, nor can one say it is not the Dharma.
That which is intended to be the Dharma is yet not the Dharma; that which is intended to be non-Dharma is yet not non-Dharma. Thus it is.
Those who come to provide realization and exposition according to circumstances have, for the most part, attained the essence that is neither existent nor non-existent.
Why is this so? Because all worthy sages and saints are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
However, the reason why it cannot be grasped and cannot be described is that what is called "not dharma" and yet "not non-dharma" is as follows:

for there to be grasping and description, phenomena such as dharma and non-dharma would all belong to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), which is precisely what is meant by "conditioned dharmas" at the end of the sutra.
To be without marks and without abiding, to accord with nature spontaneously, and to be free from artificial human contrivance is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is because they are so designated. All Bodhisattvas are called "worthy" (xian), while those at the stage of the Tathāgata are called "sages" (sheng).

Neither of these titles is achieved through artificial effort or forced contrivance; rather, they are naturally realized. However, within this, there is a distinction between those who awaken first and those who awaken later.
Therefore, those who awaken later are called "worthy," while those who awaken first are called "sages. Yet, [the distinction is merely] subtle.
There is merely the discrimination of degrees of difference. The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the essence of self-realization;
differentiation is the function of transforming the mundane. Although human differences vary, the unconditioned nature of the Dharma remains the same.
Since the Dharma is solely unconditioned, it cannot be grasped and cannot be described. How can one harbor doubts about it because humans possess differences? No.

This serves to illuminate the preceding phrase on "pure faith. When pure, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); when impure, it arises in a state of chaotic confusion, and one becomes overwhelmed by the task of managing it.
Chapter Eight: The Section on Being Born According to the Dharma.

The Buddha said that if there is someone who can receive and uphold even a single phrase from the chapters and verses of the Prajñāpāramitā up to countless phrases, they will not only surpass the merit of giving away the seven treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
one should know that within the essence of the Prajñā, all Buddhas and Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi can be produced. Therefore, it is called "born from reliance on the Dharma."

"Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One."
Why is this? This merit is not the nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.

The Buddha feared that if people heard this teaching—that it is "not to be grasped"—they would reject and discard his instructions, wondering how they could have faith and understanding, or how the Buddhas could be brought forth.
Therefore, he calculated the merit of upholding and explaining [this sutra], rather than [merely] abandoning wealth to cultivate merit.

Regarding the practice of giving and the cultivation of wisdom, this constitutes one branch of the sixfold division. Giving without dwelling on signs (*animitta*) is not intended to instruct ordinary beings who are stingy and greedy;
rather, it is specifically for those ordinary beings who have previously planted fields of merit and now possess material wealth to give.
Yet, if they only know how to seek merit and do not know how to seek wisdom, then their merit will eventually be exhausted while their karmic afflictions grow ever deeper. Therefore—
He taught him to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva. The Buddha asked:
"Suppose a person were to fill this trichiliocosm with the seven treasures, without leaving any empty space, and give it all away as a gift to plant the causes for merit in future lives."
"Is the merit obtained by this person much or not much? Subhūti replied, "It is very much.
As he followed his own inquiry into the reason for its being so great, he answered himself: "This gift of jewels is merely a worldly matter of merit;
it is not the nature of the merit of Prajñāpāramitā. If merit were based upon a fixed nature, where else could one calculate it?"
Regarding the quantity [of merit], the Tathāgata speaks from the perspective of phenomenal characteristics; thus he says that the merit of giving jewels is great.
Because it is finite, one can calculate its magnitude. Worldly wealth is exhaustible, and merit is likewise exhaustible;
one may only reckon it as being extremely vast, but it cannot be called immeasurable (*apramāṇa*). Both this question and answer employ provisional expressions. *The mind is pure and form is empty.*

Just as a mirror free from dust and obscurations perceives forms through a pure mind—just as a mirror without obscuration can manifest all images—so too do people give rise to deluded minds based on their physical bodies, thereby discriminating between "self" and "other.

Toward all agreeable objects they give rise to greed, and toward disagreeable objects they give rise to anger; thus, while striving to protect themselves, they instead undergo the toil and suffering of afflictions. Its...
This is called delusion (*moha*). Greed, hatred, and delusion destroy one's true nature (*prakṛti*). One should reflect that among the people of this world, there is none who does not die;

yet after death, the spiritual essence (*jīva*) cannot perish. Therefore, Buddhism teaches people to cultivate the nature of merit and virtue, for it is because of this nature that one can remain constant throughout kalpas.
The sutra reveals this word "nature" at this single point; in fact, throughout the entire sutra...
He said: "It is not that I am requiring people to see their nature. The area illuminated by the sun and moon constitutes a small world.
In its center is Mount Sumeru, around which the sun and moon revolve. To the south is Jambudvīpa; to the west is Aparagoyānī;
to the north is Uttarakuru; and to the east is Pūrvavideha. These are called the four continents. Thus do the sun and moon revolve."
[Śakra] travels here, situated at the midpoint of this mountain. This mountain rises higher than the sun and moon.

The summit is divided into four directions, with eight locations in each direction and one additional location in the center, totaling thirty-three locations; these are called the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa).
The sun and moon revolve over the four continents; this is called a small world-system (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*).
One thousand such small world-systems constitute a small thousand-fold world-system. One thousand such small thousand-fold world-systems constitute a middle thousand-fold world-system.

One thousand such middle thousand-fold world-systems constitute a great thousand-fold world-system. Because the term "thousand" is repeated three times, it is called the "trichiliocosm" (three-thousandfold great thousand-fold world-system).
In fact, there is only one "great trichiliocosm," which is called a "great world-system. "Three thousand" is the ultimate expression for the vastness of worlds;
reaching the "great trichiliocosm" signifies that the number has reached its absolute limit. The "seven treasures" are gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, agate, pearl, and crystal.
If, furthermore, there should be someone who receives and upholds even as little as a four-line verse from this sutra and explains it for others, their merit would surpass that of the former.
World-Honored One, speaking in terms of the nature of merit, is it not solely because of upholding this sutra? If a bodhisattva, regarding this...
In the sutras, one first clarifies the mind and perceives its nature, attaining an understanding of the wondrous principle of the true mark of ultimate emptiness.
Having received it, one does not forget it in the mind; having maintained it, one does not grow weary of its long-term practice.

This may involve the entirety of a sutra, or perhaps just one, two, three, or even four lines of a verse. The term "etc. (*deng*) does not refer solely to the four-line verse. Furthermore, out of compassion...
To guide these sentient beings according to their individual capacities is the merit of one's own nature; it is inconceivable.
How could even the giving of precious things ever equal it? To uphold and recite even a small portion of this still yields immeasurable merit, let alone that which exceeds four lines.
This is the first comparison showing the superiority of the Sūtra. [Note: It does not explicitly specify what the "four lines" refer to.]

The "Speaker" intends for people to realize for themselves where the verses reside. Regarding the comparison of merit from upholding the sutra, there are seven points, each intended as a distinct consideration:
1. Giving away treasures filling the entire world does not equal the merit of upholding this sutra. 2.

Giving away treasures from worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges increases the scope of the offering even further. 3. Giving away one's body and life as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—[does not equal it].
And [the merit of] upholding the sutra. Fourth, by giving away one's immeasurable body and life three times a day, it becomes even more extensive.

Fifth, because the offerings made by the World-Honored One during his previous lives to various Buddhas were still not equal to upholding the sutra, the cause of Buddhahood is further augmented by this compared to mere giving.
Thus, there are two instances of external wealth, two instances of internal wealth, and one instance of the cause of Buddhahood—such is the comparison.
This is already the limit. Therefore, the latter two instances state that they cannot be reached by calculation or analogy. Furthermore, there are two other points of similarity:
first, seeing that the sūtra mentions wholesome dharmas that ought to be cultivated; second, seeing that the act of expounding and instructing others is meritorious.
It is not that there is further praise or comparison, but rather that the meaning is reiterated for emphasis.
Why is this? Subhūti, all Buddhas and the Dharma of the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas all issue forth from this sūtra.
Why is it that the merit obtained by one who upholds this sutra surpasses that of bestowing precious gifts?
One must know that among all Buddhas of the past and present, there is no Buddha who did not attain all the fruits of the path through Prajñāpāramitā.

By receiving and upholding this sutra, afflictions are spontaneously severed and wondrous wisdom is spontaneously renewed. This wondrous wisdom is the Dharma-body of all Buddhas; thus, the Buddhas arise from this sutra.
It emerges. All Buddhas of the past and present possess the true wisdom of *prajñā* and guide sentient beings by teaching the Dharma in accordance with conditions.
This arises from the Bodhicitta; it is the very nature of Bodhi. This Dharma emerges from this sutra.
Therefore, one should know that this sutra does not merely refer to its words and phrases, but signifies the essential substance of the nature of *prajñā*. Indeed, the bodies of all Buddhas and...

The Dharma that is realized is entirely born from Prajñā. To bestow this upon others is for one Buddha to manifest as countless Buddhas and for one Dharma to be expounded as countless Dharmas. How could the merit within such a nature not be exceedingly vast?
"Subhūti, that which is called 'Buddha-dharma' is not, in fact, Buddha-dharma.
Yet, fearing that you might still cling to the notion of Buddha-dharma, he calls out again and says:
'That which is called Buddha-dharma is so named because the Buddha attained it while others have not; however, in reality, it is possessed by every person. The Buddha..."
Fundamentally, there is no Buddha, nor is there any dharma that is not the dharma. The Buddha-dharma does not transcend the daily activities of sentient beings.

By all means, do not grasp at various signs as being the Buddha-dharma and seek it outwardly. You must personally realize your own original nature and attain a transcendent awakening beyond phenomena;
only when you use this to awaken others can it be called the nature of merit and virtue, and only then can it be described as "immeasurable. When one investigates to this point, it is not—
The principle that "the Dharma is neither dharma nor non-dharma" is thus made even more manifest.
○ Chapter Nine: On the One Mark and the Markless.
Subhūti said to those of the Two Vehicles: "Even those who have individually realized the four fruits of arhatship cannot avoid being stalled by what they have attained; they are unable..."
Having distanced himself from the four marks and the four views, he then described for himself how his mind was not occupied with phenomena and phenomena were not occupied with his mind;
having thus reached the state of non-contention, the Buddha praised Subhūti as the foremost among those who understand emptiness.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a stream-enterer have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One."
The statement that there are distinctions among the unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) above corresponds to the fundamental intention of the Great Seal Tathāgata.
However, fearing that those who imitate this might develop a mind of attachment, the Buddha further proceeds through the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*), from the four fruits up to the Tathāgata,
and even to the Bodhisattvas who adorn the Buddha-lands through the six perfections and myriad practices, examining each one’s views.

The solidity or emptiness of the ground is determined by whether one remains bound or has subdued the afflictions. The following three sections explain that all phenomena possessing marks are entirely false and illusory;

this indicates the manner in which even unconditioned dharmas possess distinctions. The human mind possesses only the method for subduing delusion, but there is no separate method for dwelling in the truth.
Therefore, as wisdom grows greater, the substance of the mind becomes increasingly empty, having nothing to grasp. Nothing.
This is what has been attained. One who has entered the stream (srotāpanna) refers to one who has first entered the gate;

having already severed the delusions of views, coarse and heavy afflictions no longer arise, and they do not receive the bodies of asuras or other such disparate classes. This is the first fruit realized by the śrāvaka. One should contemplate this thought:
when ordinary people occupy a single stage, they value the absence of discursive thought. Indeed, the intent of the sutra is simply to...

This refers to a person who has severed their discursive thoughts. When questioned as to whether one who has attained the first fruit (srotāpanna) can give rise to such a thought of realizing the fruit, asking, "Shall I obtain this fruit?
the answer is given that it is self-attained through non-appropriation. If one realizes the dharma of signlessness, there is no mind that seeks to obtain the fruit.
If there is even the slightest mind seeking to obtain the fruit, one is not called a srotāpanna; therefore, it is said:
No. ○ Each instance of the character "fruit" (*guǒ*) has its own distinction. As for "cause and fruit" (*yīnguǒ*), one obtains today's fruit by means of what was previously the cause.
As for "realizing the fruit" (*zhèngguǒ*), one obtains the fruit of the present moment by means of what is realized now.
Furthermore, the character "fruit" has two meanings: first, the fruit of certainty; second, the fruit of retribution (*vipāka*). In this context...
This should be understood through decisive resolution. That is to say, the four fruits of the bodhisattva path are all attained by means of courageous diligence and steadfast cultivation.
The various designations such as "stream-enterer" and "once-returner" precisely refer to the stages of realizing these fruits.
Why is this? A srotāpanna is called "one who has entered the stream," yet there is nothing entered.
He does not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena; thus he is called a srotāpanna.

Why is this? When a person dwells within the six sense-objects, they are immediately obstructed by the stream of ordinary beings; otherwise, they enter the stream of the sages. There is no other distinct dharma that serves as a point of entry.
Those who have first awakened to the fruit of the Way have already severed the delusions of views and departed from birth in the four realms of existence;
therefore, they escape the stream of ordinary beings and enter the stream of the sages and worthies. Upon investigation, what is this so-called "stream"? It is precisely the entry itself.
Both are transformed. Without clinging to a single thought, one knows how to enter this state. In reality, there is no "mind entering the stream" to be found;
one merely perceives that the conditions of the sensory world are fearsome. By severing thoughts, one does not enter the impure realms of the six sense-objects, and thus afflictions do not adhere.
One does not oppose the holy stream; yet, because the notion of a self has not been forgotten, this is why one is called a *srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer).
This is one bodhisattva who has newly entered the gate of the Buddha.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does a sakṛdāgāmin have the thought, "I have attained the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin"?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? A sakṛdāgāmin is so named because he returns once more."
In reality, there is no coming or going; this is called a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Next, he questioned him: "What is your thought? Can one who has attained the second fruit give rise to such a thought of prajñā as, 'Have I attained the second fruit or not?
He replied that it is accomplished spontaneously through non-apprehension. Why? Because in the desire realm there are nine grades."

Regarding the afflictions of thought (*kleśa*), those who have attained the second fruit have already progressed compared to those of the first fruit; they are called "Once-returners" (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
As for ordinary people, regarding sensory phenomena (*nimitta*), some go forth and do not return, while others come and then go back again.

This [attainer of the second fruit], however, has once gone and returned within that realm and is entirely free from lingering attachment; thus, in reality, there is no going or returning. It is only that people...
The marks still remain. There is no attainment of the two fruits of the Sakṛdāgāmin.
These are the two Bodhisattvas. Subhūti, what do you think? Can an Anāgāmin form the thought, "I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin"?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? An Anāgāmin is so called because he does not come back."
In truth, there is none who does not come; for this reason, one is called an Anāgāmin.
Again, he questioned him: "What is your intention? Can a person who has attained the third fruit produce such a thought of prajñā?"
"Have I attained the third fruit? He replied, "One realizes the fruit by means of non-appropriation. Why?

Those who have attained the third fruit have already awakened to the emptiness of both person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*). Moment by moment they do not regress from Bodhi; compared to those of the second fruit, they have advanced further.
Regarding the six sense objects and the four marks, they realize each as empty, penetrating through past and future without any obstruction."
He specifically does not go; he directly realizes that the marks of sensory objects leave no trace of coming, yet in reality there is nothing that does not come.
His mind is empty and without self, and he does not form the thought that there is a dharma of "not-coming. He does not know that he has attained this fruit;
this is the reason for the name *anāgāmin*. Nevertheless, the views of sentient beings have not yet been entirely eliminated—this is the second fruit of the *anāgāmin*.
"There is no attainment. These are the three bodhisattvas.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does an arhat have the thought, 'I have attained the path of an arhat'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One."
He pressed him further, asking, "What is your intention? Can the noble ones of the four fruits of realization give rise to such a thought of prajñā as, 'Have I attained the path of the four fruits?
Having fully realized what was to be learned, how could there be any attainment of the path? Therefore, one does not speak of attaining the fruit."

In the end, he said that he had attained the Way (*mārga*). Indeed, the fruit (*phala*) extends through all four stages. The Arhat alone is specifically designated as having "attained the Way" because he has acquired the two knowledges of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*);
since this is the ultimate limit of the Śrāvaka path, it is called the Way. Now I ask: do you know for yourself whether you have attained the Way of the four fruits?
He replied: "I have attained the Way by way of non-appropriation (*anupādāna*)."

Why is this? Because, in reality, there is no dharma called "Arhat. World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to have the thought, "I have attained the path of Arhatship," he would immediately be clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
"Arhat. This term refers to one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), meaning there is no further dharma to be learned.

Compared to the third fruit [of the path], this is a further advancement. Why is he called "beyond training"? Because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted and there are no further afflictions (*kleśa*).
Although he is named an Arhat, it appears as if the view of a self (*jīvadr̥ṣṭi*) has not yet been entirely eliminated; yet in reality, there is no dharma that can be named "Arhat."
The Arhat has no notions of opposition or conformity; subject and object are both extinguished. This is because, though they perceive the Path, they do not cling to the Path.
He addressed the World-Honored One once more, speaking in reverse: "If one were to perceive the Path and have something to which they cling, they would merely achieve the path of an Arhat;
how could they possibly escape these four marks? This would constitute a point of attachment. This is it.
Conversely, it is said that one must not be attached to the thought [of attainment].

Thus, if one were to form the thought regarding the first three fruits, such as "I have attained the fruit of Srotāpanna" and so forth, one would likewise be attached to the marks of self, person, and so on. This can be inferred by analogy.
To form the thought "I have attained this fruit" is itself attachment to marks (*nimitta*). Attachment to marks is precisely grasping at that which is grasped (*grāhya*). This is...
It is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). What is now called "not forming thoughts and not clinging to marks" is precisely attaining without attainment;
it is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) because there is nothing to be grasped. Look at the character for "Dharma": all four preceding fruits are the Dharma.
Look at the character for "Way" (*mārga*): one sees that the four preceding fruits have not yet realized the Way.
“World-Honored One, the Buddha has declared that among those who have attained the samādhi of non-contention, I am the foremost.
World-Honored One, I am a first-rate Arhat free from desire. Yet, World-Honored One, I do not harbor the thought: ‘I am an Arhat free from desire.’”
This citation refers to his own realization of detachment. Since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) attained is identical, the difference lies only in the individual's personal realization.
He addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "In days past, the Buddha once declared that I alone had attained the state of being 'free from contention' (*araṇā*).
For an ordinary person, one moment of thought must clarify principle, while another moment of thought must eliminate desire; thus, these two moments of thought contend with one another."
One then engages in internal strife. If there is no strife, then principle and desire will both vanish. Not giving rise to thoughts of strife is *samādhi*. *Samādhi* is a Sanskrit term;
translated, it means "right concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*). When the human mind cannot awaken, it is obscured; by rectifying that awakening, one rectifies that obscuration.
To use what has been awakened to rectify what has not yet awakened—this is *samādhi*. It is not a matter of entering a supernatural state.

This is the meaning of that title. Among the ten great disciples, each has a particular excellence and is thus considered foremost in that regard—just as Ānanda is foremost in learning and Maudgalyāyana in supernatural powers. Yet, among those who possess this samādhi, I am declared to be the most supreme.
Not only is he the foremost among those who have attained samādhi, he is also called the greatest of all arhats who have abandoned desire.
The four subtle signs do not arise; he is unstained by craving and attachment.

Externally there are no objects of desire; internally there is no mind of desire. Having already departed from the realm of desire and reached the state of non-contention, one is thus separated from desire;
hence it is called "freedom from desire. When the Way is attained within oneself, emotional desires are completely severed.
Furthermore, regarding the progression through the four fruits [of the path], these are words with which the Buddha habitually praised Subhūti. Although Subhūti addressed the Buddha in this manner...
Grant me this: I truly do not harbor the thought, "I am one who has attained the fruit of the path by being free from desire.
I am identical to those who have previously attained the four fruits, in that we have both eliminated the mind that grasps at attainment.
World-Honored One, if I were to have the thought, "I have attained the path of Arhatship," then the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti is one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
It is because Subhūti has in reality nothing to practice that he is named Subhūti,
one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
"I" is a self-designation used by Subhūti; "Subhūti" is likewise a self-designation used by Subhūti. *Araṇa* means "quiescence":
outward signs are exhausted and the mind is stilled within; when both inner and outer are quiescent, when would it not be still?
This is another name for "non-contention" (*araṇā*). One who delights in the practice of *araṇā* is seen to excel in the practice of non-contention.

He addressed the World-Honored One again, speaking in reverse order: "If I were to give rise to the thought, 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' I would then become attached to the notion of being free from desire.
My mind would not yet be liberated, and I would immediately fall into the deluded thoughts of an ordinary person."
The World-Honored One will surely look down upon me with disdain. Among his disciples, he will certainly not declare, "I am one who delights in the practice of non-contention.
To conceive this in the mind is called "thought" (*smṛti*); to manifest it in action is called "practice" (*caryā*). Furthermore, to speak of it correctly:
although I possess such a practice, in reality, there is no practice of a mind detached from desire. This...
Reflecting on what preceded, he did not form such a thought, nor did he claim to have attained the Way;
rather, it was because his mind was free from attachment and attainment that he subsequently declared, "I have attained the state of non-contention.

For one who delights in practicing this, this section shows how Subhūti, having heard of the four fruits of the path, described how he had attained the fruit of freedom from desire through a mindless state, thereby aligning himself with the Buddha. Thus:
That the four fruits [of the path] are likewise attained through the mindless state becomes even more evident. In essence, the four fruits involve neither grasping nor attainment;
when one reaches the pinnacle of this practice of not entering the six sense-objects, that itself is unsurpassed bodhi.
Section Ten: Adorning the Pure Land.
From the Tathāgata’s single dharma of his own form, up to the nirvāṇa of the bodhisattvas, they do not give rise to a mind of dwelling.
Thus, regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one perceives nothing that can be attained; regarding the Buddha-field, one perceives no adornment.
It is like the formless Dharma-body, hidden within all forms; though as vast as Sumeru, the king of mountains, it cannot be compared to anything.
This attainment through non-attainment and this adornment through non-adornment are no different from one another.
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "What do you think? Did the Tathāgata, when he was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain any dharma?
"No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he truly obtained no dharma at all."

The preceding discourse on attaining the fruit might lead one to cling to the notion of a "single attainment. Therefore, he again poses a question based on his own realization to test whether Subhūti truly understands the meaning of the word "attainment.
Fearing that others might suspect the Buddha has some external teacher or lineage, he first causes him to reflect for himself, and then points it out directly from his own experience, saying:
"In the past, when I was with my teacher listening to the Dharma, my teacher must have certainly given me an opening of the Dharma."
[The Buddha] asked, "Do you not know whether there is any dharma to be attained? Subhūti replied that no dharma can be attained.
This is because the Dharma serves to awaken the pure mind in people; the Tathāgata was inherently pure from the beginning.

Having attained true awakening within his own fundamental nature at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, it was merely a matter of mind-sealing mind; he did not rely solely upon the transmission of a teacher.
One attains through recollection. If the mind has any attainment, it is the mark of abiding and cannot be pure. How could the Tathāgata have any attainment?

Dīpaṃkara is the Buddha Prabhāsa; this refers to when the World-Honored One received his prediction of enlightenment, at which time light was emitted from the pores of his eyes, ears, mouth, nose, and all hundred apertures, illuminating the ten directions like a lamp.
In the future, when he attains Buddhahood, he shall be named Dīpaṃkara. All eight princes became disciples of Prabhāsa and attained the Way;
the last among them to attain Buddhahood was Dīpaṃkara. The sixteen princes left the household life as śrāmaṇeras and all attained the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
the last among them was Śākyamuni. Thus, the World-Honored One attained unsurpassed bodhi.
The Dharma. He is the Dharma King of all the Śākyas. Regarding the Dharma, how could he have anything to attain? It is simply that he does not harbor a mind of attainment.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? "No, World-Honored One. Why is this?
That which is called adorning a buddha-field is actually no adornment; it is merely named 'adornment.'

The preceding section discussed the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. This [section] concerns the visualization of all Buddhas manifesting their bodies and preaching the Dharma, or further adorning the Buddha-fields.
The Buddha-field is a metaphor for the original aspiration for bodhi; adornment is a metaphor for the purity of the mind, being free from the distractions and disturbances of deviance and delusion.
The Buddha asked the Bodhisattvas, "By entering meditative absorption without dependence, do you possess this bodhicitta?
Subhūti understood the intent and replied, "In truth, there is no such mind. "Why is there no such mind? [The Buddha asked.
"Because that which is 'adorned' is the mind entering meditative absorption without clinging or dependence. As for the two words 'Buddha-field,' they refer to the entry of the bodhicitta."
The one who has attained meditative concentration says: When a person exerts control over the mind, they maintain a fraction of deliberate effort, and the mind consequently becomes unsettled.
When speaking of entering concentration, there is nothing for the mind to grasp; this is precisely what is called the Dharma of Non-action (*wuwei*).

As for the "land of the mind," it refers to the space within the heart; it is originally a fertile field. If one does not encroach upon it or diminish it, but instead nurtures and enriches it, how could it not be the Buddha-land?
Generally, when it is said that something "is not," it is because there is no difference [between them]; this serves to shatter appearances and reveal the principle.
Generally, when it is said that something is "a name," it is because it is merely a hollow sound; this serves to manifest the principle through phenomena.

When considering the Buddha’s intention in speaking of "adornment," he originally had no conceptualization of such adornment; therefore, he said it "is not adornment," yet he specifically designated it by the name "adornment."
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way:

they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on forms; they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. They should give rise to their mind by dwelling nowhere.
In the preceding passage, it was stated that there is "non-attainment" wherein even the notion of adornment is entirely absent; this mind is thus on the verge of becoming withered.
Therefore, this section speaks of the single character "birth" (*jìng*), so that one may see that all notions are empty and that the mind arises from within the void.
Subhūti and others should, in this manner, give rise to this pure mind; when the mind reaches such purity, [it is truly realized].
Thus, when the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are all severed, how could there be any form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena (*dharmas*) to dwell upon?
Regarding the "arising" of the pure mind and the "arising" of the six sense objects, these two instances of the word "arise" (*utpāda*) differ.

The former instance of "arise" means that this mind arises because within the mind there is no obstruction whatsoever; the latter instance of "arise" refers to [the mind] being defiled by the six sense objects.

The mind, in turn, is that which gives rise to its own states—whether appropriate or inappropriate; one is encouraged and the other cautioned, perfectly corresponding with one another, abiding nowhere, and without any attachment within the mind.
These eight characters are read as a continuous phrase. It does not speak of the arising of the mind, but rather of that which gives rise to the mind.
This is precisely because the mind is fundamentally empty and numinous, inherently possessing the principle of perpetual generation, specifically for this purpose.

Controlled by desire, the mechanism of life gradually fades away. When a person, at a moment when no thought arises, turns back to reflect and inwardly illumines, they perceive that within this mind there is something arising spontaneously;
it is not another mind, but the mind itself. This corresponds to the phrase "should have no abiding place.
It is entirely produced from the place where the mind is awakened. That which has no abiding place means that within the mind, there is nothing but awakening.
In every situation, one must not fail to respond or attempt to evade; rather, in all places, the arising mind is clearly awakened, and the numinous light shines forth.
How could any arising thought not be that very mind?
"Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body were as large as Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think?
Would that body be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One. Why is this? The Buddha has said that what is not a body is called a 'great body.'"
Because the minds of those with superior resolve are pure, their minds are vast. Only when a person possesses such a vast mind can they be said to possess a "vast body";
this is not a figurative statement referring to something external. One should regard the word "body" (*kāya*) as the word "mind" (*citta*).
The Buddha, wishing to expand Subhūti's mind, again asks whether his body is like Sumeru, the king of mountains. Subhūti then—
To realize the Buddha’s intention: although the form-body (*rūpakāya*) may be as vast as Mount Sumeru, it is entirely a manifestation of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Therefore, it should be called "extremely great" in the sense that the human mind is great, just as the body is great. Fearing that sentient beings would not awaken to this, he then proclaimed it himself, saying:
"What is meant by having a 'great body'? This refers to the Buddha’s own teaching that the pure mind is all-pervading.
The six voids are the subtle function of the arising mind; they do not refer to the body as a physical frame.
Taking the Dharma-realm as the body, it has no form—how could even Sumeru, the King of Mountains, serve as a metaphor for it?

This "non-body" is precisely the two characters "formless," which is the Dharma-body and also the pure true mind. When people do not purify their minds, they become defiled by the six [sense objects].
Dust. Does this not make its body small? Because it is far removed from all defilements, it is called "non-.
Because it is honored and extraordinary, it is called "great. Yet, if the mind does not abide in attachment, how could one attain this? ○ Sumeru:
A name for a mountain in the Western Regions, meaning "Wondrously High" (Miaogao). It is said to be composed of four jewels, hence "wondrous"; it stands out prominently above all others.
Feng said: "High. This mountain is the largest among the four continents, measuring three million six hundred and sixty thousand *li* in breadth.
As it is the foremost of all mountains, it is called the "King of Mountains" (*Śailarāja*). How could a human body be so vast?

The World-Honored One wished for people to realize the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) through the physical body (*rūpakāya*); therefore, he used this as a question by means of Mount Sumeru. Indeed, because of Sumeru...
Just as [Mount Sumeru] is the sovereign among all mountains, the Dharma-body is likewise the sovereign among all bodies.
This section of question and answer speaks of non-attainment; when one reaches the state where there is no adornment and the mind dwells nowhere, this mind alone becomes vast and great.
This, moreover, is another instance of the Buddha’s awakening of Subhūti.
Chapter Eleven: The Superiority of Unconditioned Merit.
This is a term indicating that the section on Adornment is not yet exhausted. It refers to the giving of the seven treasures; [if performed with] a mind that does not escape dwelling upon signs.
If one upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, there is nothing produced in the mind and no abiding in signs; this is called the superior merit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—what do you think?
"What do you think? Are all those grains of sand in the Ganges many? Subhūti replied, "Very many, World-Honored One.
Those Ganges rivers alone are already countless, let alone their sands. "Subhūti, I tell you this in truth:
if there were good sons or good daughters who, with the seven treasures, filled as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in those Ganges rivers..."
"If one were to give a thousand worlds as a gift, would the merit obtained be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One.

The Buddha told Subhūti, "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from within this sutra, should even receive and uphold a single four-line verse or the like and explain it for others, this merit would surpass the former merit."
From the four fruits down to the non-corporeal great body, it is stated section by section that the Buddha-dharma cannot be grasped.
Since the Dharma cannot be grasped, one might ask: what benefit is there in upholding this sutra?

Therefore, this second passage again compares the excellence of the sutra to demonstrate that its upholding and exposition are not in vain. What was previously called "mountains" is here called "rivers"; both are metaphorical explanations.
This section speaks emphatically of the vastness of worlds. As for the Ganges:
it is the river adjacent to the Jetavana Monastery in the Western Country (India), which flows eastward from Lake Anavatapta. It is forty *li* in circumference.
When the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, he frequently used this as a metaphor for the sake of the assembly. The Buddha asked: "As many as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River..."
"Grains of sand. Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in one such river. What do you think?
Would all those grains of sand from all those Ganges Rivers be numerous? Subhūti was thus intended to first realize the vastness of these grains of sand.
This serves as a prelude to what follows. Subhūti understands the Buddha’s intention: the Tathāgata does not speak falsely;

the Buddha possesses right and universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and perceives throughout the entirety of empty space and the whole of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, he first replies, "Very many, World-Honored One.
Yet, if even a single grain of sand from a single Gaṅgā River is such that all those Gaṅgās together are beyond calculation, how much more so are all those Gaṅgās?
"Could the grains of sand contained therein be counted? The Buddha called out, 'Suvikrāntavikrāmin (Subhūti), this metaphor is not a falsehood and may be truly believed.
I now speak to you with words of truth. While previously I spoke in general terms regarding things of the world, I am now speaking of the performance of meritorious deeds;
therefore, these are words of truth. Taking such grains of sand as the standard for all the Ganges Rivers, and within all those Ganges Rivers..."
There are grains of sand in the Ganges. Let one grain of sand equal one world-system; how many such world-systems would there be?
If a son or daughter of good family were to fill these world-systems with the seven treasures and bestow them as alms upon others, how great would that gift be?
How great would the merit obtained be? Previously, it was merely filling a single world-system; now, it is filling world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—it is even more so.
"It is incalculable. Yet, such a principle does not exist; it is merely a way of speaking to emphasize the vastness of the merit obtained. Subhūti understood the Buddha’s intention:
the sands of the Ganges are indeed beyond counting, let alone each grain of sand being a Ganges River and each Ganges River being a world-system.
If one were to practice giving on such a scale, would the merit obtained not be exceedingly great? The Buddha told Subhūti: 'If there were a virtuous person...'"
If men or women receive and uphold even four lines of verse from this teaching and explain its meaning to others,
causing them to attain clear understanding, the merit of this will endure through successive kalpas and surpass the merit of the aforementioned attachment-bound giving of jewels.
The previous statement, "In this sutra, one should receive and uphold [it], even as little as a four-line verse," refers to receiving and upholding even a four-line verse within this sutra;
it is distinct from the preceding passage which mentions both the sutra and the verses together, whereas this speaks of the verses alone.

If one sees that the merit of explaining even a single four-line verse to others is already thus immeasurable, then one cannot know how much greater the merit would be for one who upholds the entire sutra.
Generally, giving material gifts requires the seven treasures to obtain blessings;
however, as for the sutras and the verses within them, they do not depend on whether one is noble or lowly, rich or poor—anyone may uphold and recite them at will.
When people of the world dwell upon signs while practicing giving—building stupas and temples to adorn Buddha-lands—it is solely because their thoughts regarding merit and virtue are not pure.

They do not realize that the giving of wealth and treasures, regardless of whether it be for one great trichiliocosm or even for immeasurable great trichiliocosms of jewels, does not transcend the six sense objects and remains entirely within the realm of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). This is not as good as the four [verses] of this sutra.
Section: Benefiting Oneself and Others; Illuminating the Original Face; Both May Transcend Birth and Death and Accomplish the Unsurpassed Way.
Chapter Twelve: Honoring the Right Teaching.
First, one should revere the place where the Dharma is taught; second, one should revere the person who receives the Dharma;
third, one should revere the repository of the scriptures. This constitutes honoring the True Teaching.
Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place should be honored by all the world—
including its devas, humans, and asuras— as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha.
Since it has already been stated that the merit of upholding this sutra is supreme, one should know that the sutra is worthy of veneration; therefore, it is further addressed here.

Regarding "receiving, upholding, explaining, and elucidating": regardless of the location, if one explains this sutra according to whatever place one happens to be in—"even to" (*yāvat*) being a term indicating inclusion from below, and "etc.
(*ādi*) having the sense of comprehensive integration—there is not much *prajñā*; by citing a single instance, the entire purport is encompassed. Thus, [it is said] "four."
Sentences can be used to deliver sentient beings. In this context, although it is said that there is a place where the sutras reside, it is actually this very mind.
By preaching the Dharma with a pure mind, one gives rise to a pure mind in others.
All those in the world who possess a conditioned mind—such as the deities in heaven, the people of the world, and the fierce ones among the eight classes of spirits—are [included].
O Asuras, if you wish to seek their transformation and deliverance, you should properly give rise to a mind of reverence and make offerings to them.
You should regard those who preach the sutras as being lofty and eminent, like stupas enshrining śarīra;
and as being radiant and majestic, like temples housing Buddha images—there should be none whom you do not honor and worship. People merely revere stupas and temples, yet...
Do not show disrespect toward those who preach the Dharma. You must realize that those who preach the Dharma are themselves the Dharmakāya and are, in fact, stūpas and shrines;

how could they not be revered? Asura is a name for a Māra, specifically the lord of the Rākṣasa realm, who possesses great supernatural power and is able to rival the Dharma of the Tathāgata. When the Tathāgata preached the Dharma...
At that time, he arrived assuming the appearance of a bhikṣu. The Tathāgata was able to pierce through him with his eye of wisdom;
the asura had no power to deploy his magical arts. Consequently, his demonic power was reversed, and he returned from the heterodox to the orthodox.
This is why this sutra frequently mentions all devas, humans, and asuras who realize the fruit of enlightenment precisely at this time.
How much more so for anyone who is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite it in its entirety.
Subhūti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma. Wherever this sutra is located, there is a Buddha, as well as his honored disciples.
Virtuous words and wondrous meanings accord with the mind, just as oil assists fire; thus, the contemplation of the mind becomes increasingly clear.

For this reason, the terms "reciting and chanting" are added to this section. Continuing from the previous point, it is said that even by expounding but a small portion, one still receives offerings from devas and humans.
How much more so for one who is able to receive and uphold the entire text of this single sutra—reading from the scroll while seated and reciting from memory when walking.
As for such a person being honored by devas, humans, and asuras, what need is there to speak further?
One may know that this person has undoubtedly realized the nature of their own mind and has accomplished the supreme, foremost vehicle of world-transcendence.
This is a rare and marvelous Dharma; how could one not pay even greater reverence to it? This refers to the person who possesses it.

Vehicle. Why is this?

Chapter Sixteen: On the Ability to Purify Karmic Obstructions.

[The Buddha] spoke thus: "It causes people to give rise to thoughts of regression. Not knowing that being treated with contempt is also a matter within the practice of patience, [people become discouraged].

"Subhūti, one who treats [the Dharma] with contempt ruins their own diligence.

By nature, they will thus transcend and enter the stage of the Tathāgata. Subhūti,
if I were to fully describe the merit obtained by good sons and good daughters who, in the final age at the end of time,

If good men or women, during this time, uphold, read, and recite [this teaching], seeking the True Reality with their minds, they shall transcend and ascend to the shore of enlightenment.

"Complete" (具) signifies thoroughness and detail, which is the opposite of the aforementioned "summarized by way of essentials. It is not that the Tathāgata...

therefore, this concludes the wondrous state of non-abiding and signlessness mentioned above, as well as the intent that the Buddha did not provide a complete exposition. As for the remainder...
This is a comparative evaluation; however, it intends to sever doubts through a different perspective, differing from the previous sequence.

The dharma of arousing bodhicitta cannot be apprehended; furthermore, how could there be a mind that abides or a mind that is subdued?

The character "yi" (meaning) refers to the aforementioned phrase, "In reality, there are no dharmas. This means that [the teaching] arises spontaneously from the mind;

outside the mind, there are no dharmas. What, then, could be attained? It is precisely through awakening to the Tathāgata’s attainment of the Dharma that one attains it within the mind, without clinging to the teacher's Dharma as something truly attained.

If their words are correct, I shall claim that what I have attained truly resides within my own mind, rather than being merely attached to the teacher’s discourse.
All of this is devoid of the notion of self.

How much more so regarding any dharma? Examining this with careful scrutiny, one realizes that both person and phenomena are empty. When not a single thought arises, this is true subjugation.

According to the Tathāgata, all phenomena (dharmas) are empty and every state of mind (citta) is non-abiding.

The Way does not consist in thinking that one will attain Buddhahood in a future life and thus possess the name of a Buddha.

Regarding what is called "attaining no dharma," how is this non-attainment to be seen? Although all dharmas consist of a thousand branches and ten thousand strands, they are unified by a single thread.

Within suchness (*tathatā*), one cannot grasp the marks of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). To speak of all phenomena while they equally converge in the meaning of suchness is precisely like the flow of the hundred rivers.

When one reaches this point, such a mind should arise; this constitutes the mutual correspondence between what precedes and what follows.

This repeated analysis and elucidation is intended to resolve people's doubts. As for "attaining," it implies attaining from without;

In reality, the Tathāgata has no dharma by which he attains *bodhi*. Therefore, [the Buddha] called out to him and informed him, in order to correct the speech of ordinary people.
This is false. However, it cannot be said that the Tathāgata did not attain Bodhi; rather, he attained it within true nature (*dharmatā*).

Since this nature is fundamentally without dharmas, to rely upon it as something substantial would leave one with no basis whatsoever. To view it as empty, however, allows for perfect penetration at every point.
Being neither real nor empty, what dharma could possibly be applied? That which was previously described as "neither real nor empty" is merely a word.
The signlessness attained by the Tathāgata is neither real nor false; this is what is called the "dharma-less" principle established by the Tathāgata.

The method for attaining Buddhahood does not require one to seek bodhi apart from all phenomena (*dharmas*). This explains the meaning of "all phenomena are like [an illusion].
Furthermore, fearing that people might become attached to these phenomena, the Buddha addressed Subhūti: "As for what is called 'all phenomena,' they are merely used as a means for practice;

In truth, it is nothing more than a false name. One must not, within the midst of all phenomena, cling to the existence of bodhi.
Can a person become mired in dharmas and fail to know true nature?

The Buddha again asked himself: "For what reason are all sentient beings called 'sentient beings' (sattva) and not called 'enlightened beings'?

Purity is signless; it does not rely on external adornments. If one contemplates the Western [Pure Land] without attaining the One True Dharma-realm, such external adornments are not true ornamentation.

"How could a bodhisattva intentionally adorn a buddha-field?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the non-existence of self and phenomena, the Tathāgata calls him a true bodhisattva."

Saving sentient beings is great compassion; adorning the Buddha-lands is great wisdom. Both are matters within the domain of a bodhisattva. If one acts with even a single thought [of self], one is no longer a bodhisattva.

If this is so, what kind of mind must arise to be called a bodhisattva? All characteristics involve the notion of "self. For example, if one saves beings while clinging to signs and attributes the merit to oneself, or adorns the lands while clinging to signs and seeking [recognition]— [The text continues: ...this is not the way of a bodhisattva. A bodhisattva’s mind is free from all marks; it is vast and equal, like empty space. It does not dwell on the thought of saving sentient beings, nor does it dwell on the thought of adorning the Buddha-lands. Why? Because there is no self to be found. Since there is no self, how can there be anything belonging to a self? Thus, when there is no self and nothing belonging to a self, one neither grasps at the thought of saving sentient beings nor grasps at the thought of adorning the Buddha-lands. This is called the true practice of a bodhisattva. To act otherwise is to fall into the duality of subject and object, and is not the path of a bodhisattva. Therefore, a bodhisattva should cultivate a mind that is signless, ungrasping, and non-dual, and thus truly fulfill the vows of a bodhisattva.
Blessings belong to me. Now, we speak of the dharma of non-self; this is precisely the prior teaching of signlessness and non-abiding.
It must mean that one takes the bodies of all under heaven as one's self, rather than taking one's own individual body as one's self—this is "non-self in persons.
One should practice giving, not begrudging what one possesses in order to relieve others. One should practice patience, remaining free from anger even when having one's limbs severed.

Furthermore, dharmas are also without self; they are transparently luminous in every place. One who attains a mind that accords with this wondrous perfection is what the Tathāgata calls a true practitioner of cultivation, and such a person may be granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.

Within the chapter, the three previous statements were said not to be those of a Bodhisattva because they imply the existence of a self; this statement is called that of a true Bodhisattva, for it is sufficient to realize that no dharma is attained.

This is the essential meaning. Since all phenomena (*dharma*) are fundamentally non-existent, how can one seek to abide in them? When the World-Honored One reaches this point, he subsumes the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) into the single mark of the self (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*).
To eliminate these four marks, it is simply a matter of penetrating the absence of self. What follows below clarifies the intent regarding both the self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*).
Above, while discussing the six sense objects (*ṣad-viṣaya*), only the mark of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) was mentioned; this was because sound, fragrance, and so forth—
It arises from form. Although these four marks are mentioned, only the dharma of non-self is specifically taught, because the person, the multitude, and the life-span all arise from the self.
When one penetrates this, there is no obstruction between self and other; this is precisely the single mind of perfect enlightenment.
What room is there for [anything else] to constitute the Dharma?

The preceding section spoke of the five eyes; the subsequent section speaks of the three minds. In the middle, it says: "All sentient beings within the Buddha-world of Pure and Wondrous Rivers."
The Tathāgata fully knows the mind; although it varies in terms of superiority or inferiority, goodness or evil, all are like the three minds which are unattainable.
All phenomena return to the One, and within that One there is no further differentiated observation. Therefore, this section is named "Observing the Identity of the Single Essence."
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? "So it is, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye. "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? "So it is, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye. "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye? "So it is..."
“Venerable One, the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye. “Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye?
“Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye. “Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?
“Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye.”
This is the answer that subdues [the opponent]. Previously, it was stated that there is no self (*anātman*). Now, one asks about this by means of the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*).

Since the eye is also one of the faculties of the self-body, if there were no self, the characteristics of the eye would necessarily be empty. One who does not understand the characteristic of non-self merely lacks the burdens of the body;
it is not that the body itself is absent. When the burdens of the body are completely forgotten, the wisdom of the self [is revealed].
The nature [of these eyes] then permeates outward from the light of the eyes; thus, there are these five eyes. When the Buddha questioned the five faculties, his every step spoke of increasing depth.
When Subhūti answered regarding the five eyes, his every step revealed increasing height. In essence, the five eyes are collectively but one eye;
when analyzed individually, they possess degrees of depth, yet when integrated as a whole, they are without high or low. This is the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).
This refers to the eye of the physical body (*rūpakāya*). When a person possesses a physical body, they are endowed with this eye;
yet, that some see what is correct while others see what is erroneous is due to the vast difference between these two types of fleshly eyes. Ordinary people and the Tathāgata share this same eye.
The Tathāgata possesses this, and by means of this eye, he is able to realize the supreme fruit; thus it may be called the Tathāgata’s fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).
As for the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), it can universally illuminate the deviant and the correct among sentient beings, like looking down from a high vantage point.
Every minute detail is seen in its entirety; this is realized through the fleshly eye after attaining the fruit. As for the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*):

the Tathāgata possesses the light of wisdom spanning the three periods of time, whereby he does not merely perceive the arising and ceasing, or the coming and going, of his own person alone, but clearly discerns the various forms and characteristics of all sentient beings;
this is perceived from within the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*). As for the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*): that which it beholds follows a single track.
Regarding the Dharma, one must not again fall into delusion concerning what is contrary to it.
Thus, the Tathāgata once used this eye to see through the asuras’ feigned path that confuses the true for the false, causing them to turn back from Māra and enter the Right Path.
The Buddha-eye sees that all sentient beings can attain Buddhahood, without any distinction between good and evil; it is precisely this opening of the eyes out of compassion for sentient beings.
When his eyes are closed, they encompass the entire Dharma-realm, yet there is nothing that does not enter those eyes.
Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the grains of sand in the Ganges River truly sand?
“Yes, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata says they are sand. Subhūti, what do you think? As for a single Ganges River...

"Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in all those rivers. If there were as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers, would they be numerous?
"They would be very numerous, World-Honored One."
Although Subhūti knows that the Tathāgata possesses the five eyes, he does not yet know that the Tathāgata perceives the minds of sentient beings with his eye;
therefore, he asks again: "What is your understanding of this? The passage beginning with "All those in the Ganges" consists of five successive layers:
