This serves primarily to inspire Subhūti to realize the state of the "unified totality" (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*). Previously, it was stated that the thirty-two marks cannot be perceived;
here, the question is raised again as to whether the Tathāgata can be viewed by means of these marks. This is precisely intended for Subhūti to clearly recognize [the true nature of the Buddha].
One should perceive the Tathāgata through his physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*). It is thus, it is thus; this is the capacity of one who welcomes the Tathāgata.

For the time being, following the Buddha’s lead, he speaks of perceiving the Tathāgata by means of his marks. Fearing that [the listener] might become attached to the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and fail to realize the essence of the Dharma (*dharmatā*), the Buddha further raises the difficulty of the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) being none other than the Tathāgata. "Turning the wheel" refers to the Wheel of the Dharma (*dharmacakra*); [he is] the Wheel-Turning King.
He governs the four continents; since his merit and karma are likewise vast, he too possesses the thirty-two marks of a Buddha.

If one were to perceive the Tathāgata by means of these marks, then a wheel-turning monarch would also have to be a Buddha. How could one know that the marks of a Buddha manifest from the Dharma-body, whereas the marks of a king arise from karmic causes?
Though they appear similar, they are in fact different. How can one argue based on their physical marks? Subhūti was deluded.

Xin suddenly offered an interpretation, saying: "As I understand the meaning of the Wheel-Turning King as taught by the Buddha, although a Wheel-Turning King cultivates the thirty-two marks, he ultimately does not accord with the pure, original mind.
Therefore, he cannot yet be designated as a Tathāgata; furthermore, a Tathāgata should not be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks. [The preceding section discusses "seeing."]
“The Tathāgata”—this causes Subhūti to fix his gaze with one eye; this is said to be the contemplation of the Tathāgata.
This causes Subhūti to concentrate his mind with single-minded devotion. The former [explanation] refers to the external, while the latter refers to the internal;

such is the difference in the interpretation of these two characters. Therefore, although Subhūti has already responded in this manner, he further realizes that it is not appropriate. In short, in reality...
One should not seek the meaning of the mind externally.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses.
Subhūti was thus able to understand the difficult meaning of the Buddha’s intent, and the Buddha then spoke these verses to confirm it.
"If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person walks a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.

The essence of the Dharma-body is not separate from sound and form; yet, one must not seek to recognize the "Self" within the thirty-two marks, claiming that this is the true self, which is the Buddha-nature.
The Buddha does not manifest body or mind within the triple world—how could it be...
One perceives [the Buddha] by means of the marks and signs of radiance. For forty-nine years, he did not speak a single word;

how, then, could one seek him through the hearing or reception of written characters? If one perceives him through physical forms or seeks him through sounds, one immediately loses the essence of true emptiness and formlessness, mistakenly entering onto a deviant path. How, then, could one see the true countenance of the Tathāgata? This is profound.
This refutes the error of clinging to appearances. One should see that people ought to withdraw their gaze and turn back their hearing, practicing in accordance with the true nature.
One must not seek the Tathāgata within the realm of illusory forms and sounds.
Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Nature of Prajñā is Neither Ceasing Nor Extinct. The essence of prajñā is detached from all dharmas and all marks.

If one does not awaken to the principle that it is neither ceasing nor extinct, then to say it exists is to fall into the view of eternalism, and to say it does not exist is to fall into the view of nihilism; both lose the middle way of prajñā.
It is the Way, Subhūti.

If you should have this thought: "The Tathāgata has not attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of perfection," Subhūti, do not have such a thought. The Tathāgata has not [attained it] by means of the marks of perfection.

Therefore, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti, if you should think that those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* teach the annihilation of all phenomena, do not hold such a thought.
Why is this? Those who have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding phenomena.
Since the physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) cannot be grasped as a means to contemplate the Tathāgata, how much less could one attain *bodhi* by taking them as an object of cognition?

The Buddha further feared that those who contemplate the Tathāgata by way of the absence of marks might say that if the person is empty, then phenomena are also empty, ultimately falling into the view of annihilationism.
Therefore, he spoke this so that one may perceive bodhi without being obstructed by various marks; this is precisely what is meant by "neither real nor false.
The emphasis lies solely on the three characters "annihilationism" (*duanmie*). Since the Tathāgata possesses these marks, yet does not [appear] as a single mark...
It exists of itself; therefore, there is nowhere it is not fully present. This "mindfulness" refers to contemplating the Tathāgata through the characteristic of arising.
The repeated statements regarding "acting" and "not acting" serve to clarify that one must not become mired in physical forms or vocal sounds.
"If one acts" points out the error; "do not act" opens the way for awakening. Fully complete.
"Characteristics. This refers to the characteristics of merit. The Buddha first turned his words around, saying:
"If you harbor such thoughts of grasping at characteristics, then the Tathāgata did not originally attain bodhi by means of the marks of perfection.

He then corrected his words, saying: "Do not give rise to such thoughts of attachment to characteristics. The Tathāgata did not originally attain bodhi by means of the marks of perfection. Characteristics are external..."
"Characteristics. Bodhi is the true nature; how could it be attained by means of external characteristics?
This clarifies the preceding passage and represents the point where the Buddha speaks with earnest and repeated exhortation. The Buddha then reverses his phrasing and says:

"If you were to conceive such thoughts and resolve to generate the bodhicitta, you would cast aside all dharmas, severing them and not employing them, as when one speaks of the physical marks of the Buddha-body."
Illusory forms ultimately belong to that which is subject to exhaustion; it is for this reason of cessation that [the Buddha] spoke thus. The Buddha further rectified his phrasing and showed him:
"One must not entertain such a thought. Why must one not entertain such a thought?

It is because those who have resolved to seek the true nature must practice according to the various dharmas of giving, patience, and so forth; they must not, however, bring about the total extinction of the Buddha-dharma.
One should know that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the essence of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and the conditioned is the function of the unconditioned.
Therefore, those who do not employ dharmas take the characteristic of cessation as their principle; this is obtained through the mind. Why concern oneself with external characteristics?

Since dharmas are realized by means of the mind, how could they be subject to cessation? As for the causes of merit cultivated in the Mahāyāna and the fruits of merit thereby attained, they merely involve detachment from...

The characteristic of grasping and attachment is not the same as the nihilistic view of the Lesser Vehicle; therefore, it is said that regarding phenomena, one does not speak of a characteristic of annihilation.

The previous [passage] opened up the door to the characteristic of attachment for those who have already crossed over; this [passage] opens up the door to the view of annihilation for those who have not yet crossed over.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: On Non-Attachment and Non-Greed.
The Buddha said: "Because one upholds Prajñā, one realizes that all dharmas are without self and is able to achieve the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
How could the merit of a person who gives the seven treasures ever be compared to this? As for that [former] giving..."
There is the experience of craving; this experience of non-craving held by the upholder of the sūtra is called "right experience" because it does not grasp.
It is like the ocean receiving the hundred rivers—how could there be any sense of "self" therein?

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to take seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them in charity, and if another person were to know that all phenomena are without self and thereby attain patience (kṣānti), this bodhisattva would surpass the merit obtained by the former bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because bodhisattvas do not accept meritorious virtue (puṇya).
Subhūti said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, why does a bodhisattva not accept merit?
“Subhūti, the merit performed by a bodhisattva should not be clung to with greed; for this reason, it is said that they do not accept merit.”
Now, although all dharmas should not be annihilated, they likewise must not be clung to.

Here, I do not compare this with those who uphold the sutra, but rather with those who have attained the Dharma, thereby describing the wondrousness of the Buddha-dharma. The character "receive" (shòu) in "receiving merit" (shòu fúdé) corresponds to the two characters "giving" (bǎoshī) above;
for that which is given results in that which is received. Furthermore, the character "to act" (zuò) corresponds [to the preceding context].

The character "receive" (shòu) appears above. Because of what is received, one perceives what is performed. This section again borrows from the discourse on giving (*dāna*) to explain how patience (*kṣānti*) is accomplished;
it does not emphasize giving itself. Previously, giving was attributed to sentient beings; here, it is further attributed to the Bodhisattva.
This does not mean that the Bodhisattva abandons giving; rather, it is precisely through this that the *bodhicitta* is verified.

Listen! Even if a bodhisattva were to give away worlds as numerous as infinite as space filled with jewels, this would still be far more than a heap [of merit] equal to Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains.
This is solely because of a single thought of giving while attached to signs, desiring to receive a reward of fortune;

thus one falls into the minor fruits of the human or celestial realms and cannot accomplish the virtues of one's own nature. Furthermore, if there is someone who understands that which was previously explained—this one...
All phenomena are simply the exhaustion of non-self. That by which they are accomplished lies in the ability to endure. "Endurance" (kṣānti) carries the meaning of firmness and immovability;
it refers to the aforementioned absence of contention, all wholesome dharmas, and the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
It is only because people cannot endure that they fail to achieve accomplishment. Through endurance, one [overcomes] the attachment to the six sense objects.
When the mind is entirely firm and free from outflows, it can restrain delusive thoughts so that they do not arise;

one may then set each thing down one by one until both person and phenomena are realized as empty. When wisdom merges with principle, this is precisely what constitutes the attainment of patience (*kṣānti*).

For the Buddha does not save the world through impatience, but through patience he relinquishes the self. To possess great patience toward oneself is precisely what enables one to be greatly impatient toward others.

In this world, having attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), he is fundamentally different from those who practice giving while abiding in the characteristics of conditioned existence.
How could the unconditioned merit obtained by this bodhisattva not be far superior to the conditioned merit of bestowing jewels?
Yet, for what reason is that which is obtained superior to the former? It is because the one who attains it is free from the notion of "mine" (*mama*).
It is inherently possessed; it does not depend on external acquisition, nor is it a case of one person giving and another receiving.

This is because a Bodhisattva does not accept the retribution of tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena. Furthermore, Subhūti may wonder: "If merit must necessarily yield results, why say they are not accepted?
One should know that what is meant by "not accepting" is not that they reject and refuse them. These are my own inherent possessions; they are not bestowed upon me by others.
Where could there be room for its reception? Merit is its very nature; it neither increases nor decreases. From what, then, could it be received?
Therefore, it is further said that a bodhisattva "should not greedily cling to the merit they have performed. Merit is created by oneself and received by oneself.
If one regards it as "mine" and seeks to increase one's store of merit, then one is greedy. This word "greed" (貪) must be understood in this sense.
Since there are distinctions among the unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) above, one knows that the conditioned sphere (*saṃskṛta-pada*) is precisely craving (*rāga*).
As for craving, there is nothing that does not cling to signs (*nimitta*). This is why the Bodhisattva does not accept [them].
Chapter Twenty-nine: The Stillness of Dignified Conduct.
The essence of Prajñā-wisdom is profoundly still and eternally quiescent like the empty space of the ten directions; yet it does not reject any phenomena.

It is quiescent while constantly illuminating, and illuminating while constantly quiescent. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—amidst these four modes of dignified conduct—it abides eternally in nirvāṇa.
There is nothing that is not pure; therefore, this aspect is called the tranquility of deportment.

Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught. Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. Therefore...
He is named Tathāgata.
The previous statement that one should not be greedily attached implies that even the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are especially not to be clung to.

The preceding section discussed the physical marks of the Buddha’s body; this section discusses the functioning within those physical marks. This paragraph employs the four postures—coming, going, sitting, and lying down—[to illustrate this].
The character "Juo" (若) is used as a metaphor for the intention of the Tathāgata. Fourth, regarding the character "Juo": it signifies that there is truly no coming, going, sitting, or reclining.

People believe only that the Tathāgata possesses form and color; thus, if a single thought of his "coming" suddenly arises in their minds, they immediately perceive him as having come, and acts of gazing upon, prostrating to, and reverently honoring him ensue. If, however, a single thought of his "going" arises...
If it were as you suggest, then the doctrine of withered meditation and desiccated nature would arise.

If one were to maintain mindfulness while sitting or lying down and thereby consider oneself as actually sitting or lying there, then upon encountering any stupa or temple, one would immediately claim that the Tathāgata is seated or reclining therein, and the notion of relying upon such [external objects] would again arise. Therefore, in general, you do not understand the meaning of what has been taught.
To resolve the confusion of later generations: the two lines "having nowhere from which it comes" do not form a formal antithesis; the second line merely serves as a supplementary remark.
The term "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One) means coming according to one's true nature, which carries the sense of being innate and co-emergent with birth;

it does not mean that at the time of coming, there was absolutely nowhere from which he came. However, this nature is empty and numinous; if one were to ask from where its starting point originates, [it would be beyond description].

Consequently, there is a shadow. Thus, it is said that there is "nothing" (*wu suo*). In the second phrase, by examining the character "also" (*yi*), one knows that the Buddha spoke only of the Tathāgata, and never of the Tathāgata-gone.
"Coming" (*lai*) refers to where one has come from; "going" (*qu*) refers to where one goes.
This is because that from which one has come is precisely what one returns to when going. As for "coming," it means coming in its entirety. Going... [text ends]
It departs without deficiency; even if it returns after having departed, it remains exactly as it was.
How can this not be called the Tathāgata? From the minute and subtle atom to the vast world, whether in division or combination, there is nothing that does not conform to this principle.
The following text then elaborates upon this in detail.
Section Thirty: Harmonizing with Principle and Characteristics.
The Buddha refers to the world of atoms as the phenomenal aspect (*shixiang*). That which can contain these atoms is the rational nature (*lixing*).

Phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and fundamental nature (*dharmatā*) are blended into one, with nothing that can be divided. Ordinary beings are greedily attached to phenomenal characteristics and fail to awaken to fundamental nature;
thus, they pursue birth and extinction while failing to investigate nirvāṇa. It would be impossible not to speak of this as being without interruption.
"Subhūti, if a good man or a good woman were to grind the trichiliocosm into a mass of fine dust, what do you think?
Would that mass of fine dust be numerous? Subhūti replied, "It would be very numerous, World-Honored One. Why is this?
If that mass of fine dust were substantially real, the Buddha would not have called it a 'mass of fine dust.'"
Why is this? The Buddha said that the multitude of atoms is not, in fact, a multitude of atoms; it is merely designated as a "multitude of atoms.
This, together with what follows, elucidates the meaning of the atom and the world.

To speak of atoms and to speak of worlds is to say that what is small cannot contain even a single mustard seed, while what is large can hide Mount Sumeru; yet the forms of both the small and the large are ultimately [unreal].
To clarify this further, it is reiterated once more: the world is originally composed of a collection of dust.

It is not that the world is physically broken down into minute particles; rather, the current mention of "breaking" refers to deluded thoughts, indicating merely the perception of something being created.
A student of the Way who does not realize that all phenomena are empty divides the vast world in a single thought-moment.

"Separate them. Let the egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born beings be in their chaotic confusion; analyze them until they become fine dust. What do you think? Would these not be many?

This was used to develop Subhūti’s understanding by means of something easily comprehensible to people. [Subhūti] replied, having realized it: "The dust would be exceedingly many," using this as a metaphor for the activities of the *nirmāṇakāya* throughout the ages.
[The Buddha said: "If one were to shatter the world-system into fine dust, [using the perspective of an ordinary person...]"
If one were to measure them with the mind, they would be too numerous to surpass. Again, he addressed the World-Honored One and asked himself:
"For what reason are those motes of dust so exceedingly many? He answered himself: "The abundance of these motes of dust is nothing other than a construction of shadows, echoes, and falsehoods.
If the multitude of motes of dust were truly existent, the Buddha would not have spoken of crushing them into motes of dust. This is because...

This means that if one were to claim that true nature exists as a substantial reality, it could not be described; yet, since the multitude of atoms does not exist as a substantial reality, the Buddha spoke of them.
Thus, all that can be described is false and illusory, which is why it is said to be "inexpressible" and "ungraspable.
Furthermore, when he asks himself the reason why he does not speak of this multitude of atoms, he answers for himself: "That which the Buddha speaks of is [like] a pulverized..."
The world is composed of a multitude of subtle particles (*paramāṇu*). It disperses with the wind and coagulates with water; it has no fixed essence. Can it be grasped as something real?
If one attempts to grasp it, there is nothing to grasp; if one seeks to separate from it, there is no necessity for separation—it is merely the name "a multitude of subtle particles.
To know this is to know that whether the Nirmāṇakāya of the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, [it is likewise without fixed substance].
"However, responding to the world while remaining in emptiness—World-Honored One, that which the Tathāgata has called the 'trichiliocosm' is not a world; it is merely named a world."
The world is another name for the body. Subhūti realized the subtle dust and, by extension, realized the world.
Although the realm is vast, its cycles of primal assembly, evolution, and dissolution span a total of 129,600 years; even heaven and earth come to an end.
It is not a world; it is merely that this world is so named. Thus, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata neither comes nor goes, yet it does not fail to dwell in the world, being wondrously empty.
Why is this? If a world were truly existent, it would be a unified whole (*piṇḍagraha*).
What the Tathāgata calls a unified whole is not a unified whole; it is merely designated as a unified whole.
Furthermore, he asks himself why the world is not real. He answers:
"If the world were truly existent, it would be formed by an aggregation of atoms, and the world would be established upon those many atoms as a phenomenon of composite unity;
thus, there would be no way to attain liberation. 'Composite unity' means that once unified, it can never be disintegrated again."
This is a matter of division. Before there is any matter of conjunction, the mind of conjunction first arises. When the mind conjoins with the matter, they take form in relation to one another.
It is just like the ears, eyes, mouth, and nose: before a single thought arises, colors, sounds, fragrances, and flavors are entirely without form.

When a thought arises and one wishes to see, one then conjoins with the characteristic of form (*rūpa-nimitta*). When a thought arises and one wishes to hear, one then conjoins with the characteristic of sound (*śabda-nimitta*).
When a thought arises and one wishes for the mouth and nose to accord with one’s intent, one then conjoins with the characteristics of fragrance and taste (*gandha- and rasa-nimitta*).

All this originates from a single thought, which subsequently becomes entangled with the characteristics of phenomena. The Tathāgata has constantly taught that [this occurs] in a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*).
The characteristics are not so. Since the Tathāgata is empty of phenomenal marks (*nimitta*), that which remains is the true nature (*dharmatā*). Both are free from attachment;
within this, there exists naturally the principle of union without seeking it.
To contain the world within a single atom, it is fully present within that one atom without any remainder being perceived. To contain an atom within the world, each and every atom...

Within each mote of dust, the worlds of the ten directions appear individually, yet there is no sense of insufficiency; they are neither joined nor separated—this is called the "single unified mark" (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*).
How could there ever be such a single unified mark that could be named? Whenever it is said "it is not," it means that in reality it does not exist;
whenever it is said "this is its name," it means it is merely a provisional designation. The preceding discussion concerned the motes of dust, the worlds, and the marks of the Buddha.
Discussing these, they are all not real, and in principle there is nothing that can be said. This is because one perceives that the Tathāgata is beyond description;
this arises from the Buddha-body and the world of atoms. Discussing these, they are all without reality and alike return to emptiness.
This is because one perceives that the greedy person does not know emptiness.
Subhūti, that which is a "unified whole" (ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa) is inexpressible; yet ordinary worldlings greedily cling to such things.
Fearing that people might give rise to false attachments, the Buddha has swept away even the notion of a unified whole. This is what the Buddha meant by this principle.

One must wait for those who have attained awakening; if one explains by means of words and speech, it is not only the ordinary beings of middling and lower capacities who explain atoms while clinging to atoms, or explain worlds while clinging to worlds—even ordinary beings of superior faculties explain the "unified whole" while clinging to the unified whole.
How could they possibly transcend and awaken? "Phenomena" (*shi*) are spoken of in contrast to "principle" (*li*); true nature is both principle and phenomena.

They move freely and without obstruction. Ordinary people do not understand true nature; they falsely attach themselves to the phenomena of the five aggregates and six sense organs that manifest within nature.
Clinging to them, they refuse to sever these attachments. They mistake the physical body for the self and sink into the six realms of existence, having no means of escape.
This is why they are unable to empty the world and reduce it to the size of a minute mote of dust.
To speak of them as a unity is like glue or lacquer adhering to an object: at first they do not join, but as soon as they do, they become so firm that they cannot be separated.
Thus, the aspect of "union" is easily clung to with greed. As for "unity," this refers to the initial thought-moment.
Once that initial thought arises, one is joined to it until the very end, remaining immersed in delusion; therefore, such a person is called an "ordinary being" (*pṛthagjana*). It is just like this.
The meaning of "there is nothing to be said regarding what comes" has been fully elucidated here.
Chapter Thirty-one: On the Non-arising of Knowledge and Vision.
The Buddha said: "Those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta should know, see, and believe that all dharmas are without marks (animitta) in this manner. Self-...
Yet, among these four marks, no cognition or vision arises.
Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Buddha taught the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span, what do you think, Subhūti?
Does this person understand the meaning of what I have said? "No, World-Honored One. This person does not."

One understands the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught. Why is this? When the World-Honored One speaks of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span, these are not actually views of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span;
they are merely designated as "the view of a self," "the view of a person," "the view of a sentient being," and "the view of a life-span."
The following clarifies the departure from the two views of self and phenomena. This section first addresses the departure from the view of self.
In the "Chapter on Subduing" at the beginning of the sutra, it is said that if a bodhisattva thinks there are beings to be saved, they are attached to the four marks (*catvāri nimittāni*).

In the "Chapter on Abiding," it is said that if the mind grasps at marks, one is attached to the four marks. These four marks are the very attachments to be relinquished throughout this entire sutra; therefore, the Buddha asks Subhūti:
If someone were to say that the Buddha has taught in various places that there are four views, Subhūti, you should consider this:
can you understand whether the meaning taken by the Buddha in these words is necessarily different from the four views held by worldly people?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One, because the Tathāgata possesses the four true views which differ from those of ordinary people. The World-Honored One said, "Ordinary people..."

The habit of delusion manifests as "marks" (nimitta) within objects and as "views" (dṛṣṭi) within the sense faculties. Because one does not abide in marks externally, it fundamentally follows that one does not abide in the faculties internally.
When worldly people perceive these marks without transforming them, they possess no true vision; their seeing is as if they do not see.
How, then, can they understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught? As for the meaning of what he taught, World-Honored One, the so-called "four true views" are in fact not [true] views.
Ordinary people possess the four deluded views of self and non-self, love and hate, and longevity and brevity;

if such a person clearly realizes that truth arises from delusion and delusion arises from truth, and that truth and delusion cannot be distinguished but merge into one, [then they have attained realization].
These are called the four views. What are the true four views? When the Tathāgata says that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, this is the true view of self (*ātman*).
When he says that all sentient beings possess the nature of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), this is the true view of person (*pudgala*).
To say that all sentient beings are fundamentally free from afflictions is the view of a true sentient being.

To say that the original nature of all sentient beings is indestructible throughout ten thousand kalpas is the view of a true self-entity (jīva). The preceding discussion concerned the marks of "self," "person," and so forth, whereas this discussion concerns views, which differ from those marks.
To speak of "marks" implies that some mark still remains; to speak of "views" implies that even non-existence and the absence of marks are absent.

This is what is meant by "seeing. This seeing is not seen by the eyes, but is seen directly by the mind. When the mind possesses this seeing, then even though the marks (lakṣaṇa) do not exist, they nevertheless cling to existence.
The Tathāgata spoke these words because he feared that later generations might mistakenly believe the Tathāgata’s teaching to imply that there are four kinds of seeing;
thus, he wished to forcibly lead them back to non-existence and therefore reiterated his statement.

Subhūti, those who have set their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, regarding all dharmas, know them thus, see them thus, and resolve upon them with faith thus, so that they do not give rise to the notion of dharmas (*dharma-saṃjñā*).
Subhūti, as for what is called the "notion of dharmas," the Tathāgata says it is not a notion of dharmas; it is merely designated as the "notion of dharmas."
This is the departure from views regarding phenomena (*dharmadṛṣṭi*). Within ultimate perfect awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), how could there be the names of the four marks?
"The three suchnesses" refers to the bodhicitta; it corresponds to the preceding [passages] on "how should one dwell? and the phrase "thus dwelling.
"Not giving rise to the marks of phenomena" corresponds to the preceding [passages] on "how should one subdue [the mind]? and "thus subduing. For when the marks of phenomena do not arise, then...
